CONSTRAINT THIS PUTS ON THE STATIC SEARCH, which is the part worth acting on: an ov12 address
below 0x021C13B0 does not contain ov12's code in battle. Anything above it does -- the intact
region holds both code (a `bx` at file offset 0x01D70D+6) and strings ("elayMess" near 0x027AE5).
So ov12 code IS executable in battle, but only above the boundary. Any hypothesis resting on ov12
code below 0x021C13B0 is dead without further argument.

THE AMBIENT ELEMENT IS CONFIRMED WHERE STATIC INFERRED. r3 = 0x021BA4B0 is file offset 0xE2F0,
inside the OVERWRITTEN low region. Live bytes there:
  04 02 00 00 02 00 00 00 20 04 00 00 02 00 00 1C
which reads as a typed descriptor -- +0x04 = 2 is the base damage byte and +0x0E = 0 is the class
index, both re-read live and matching the nine captured stops. So the element is a real structure

Also note the boundary bytes carry pointers: E0 77 1D 02 is 0x021D77E0 and AC C6 1A 02 is

CAVEAT ON MY OWN NUMBER: 48% intact against the doc's 59.6% resident. The boundary is exact but
the two figures are measuring different things and I have not reconciled them -- the doc may count

comments.author: djdjo
comments.text:
CAVEAT ADDED AGAINST THIS BEAD'S HEADLINE NUMBER, prompted by jus-ov12-boundary-probably-moves-05o. If the boundary moves with allocation history, then 0x021C13B0 is not a measurement of a boundary -- a monotone bisection cannot detect a moving target, because it never re-probes a point it has already used to set lo or hi. The search converges and returns a value regardless, and that value has no defined meaning if the predicate is time-varying. I reported it as an exact boundary at 16-byte resolution and that precision is only justified if the boundary is stable, which is exactly what is now in question.

The 32-sample sweep has the same exposure: it establishes that SOME split existed during the sweep, and the clean 15/15-above, 0/17-below pattern is hard to produce from a randomly drifting target, but it does not pin the split's location in time.

What survives regardless of movement: the base is correct (the upper region is byte-identical to the file at its declared address, which a shift cannot produce), the split is contiguous rather than scattered, ov12's entry point at offset 0 is overwritten, and the ambient element at 0x021BA4B0 sits in overwritten territory. Those are qualitative and do not depend on where exactly the boundary sat.

What does NOT survive: the specific address, and the 48% figure derived from it.

title: ov12's battle boundary is probably a MOVING high-water mark, not page granularity -- and coincidence cannot explain the 59.6/48 gap
description:
Runtime found ov12's battle window splits contiguously at 0x021C13B0 -- 84.5 KB overwritten
below (including ov12's entry point at offset 0), 79.4 KB byte-identical above, at its declared
address. They measured 48% intact, the residency doc says 59.6%, and they flagged the gap
unreconciled with a guess of page granularity. Taking the reconciliation, because it produces a
falsifiable prediction and a warning.

PAGE GRANULARITY IS OUT. 0x021C13B0 is 0x3B0 into its page -- not aligned to 0x1000, nor to
0x20. It IS aligned to 0x10. Sixteen-byte granularity is an allocator, not a pager.

COINCIDENTAL BYTE MATCHING IS ALSO OUT, and this is the part that matters. For 59.6% and 48.4%
to describe one memory state, 18,730 of the 86,512 overwritten bytes would have to match the
file by accident -- 21.7%. They cannot:
  - ov12's file content in the low region is only 10.0% 0x00 bytes, so zero-on-zero matching
    caps out at 10.0% even if the live region were ALL zeros
  - random agreement on the remaining ~90% adds roughly 0.4%
  - ceiling therefore ~10.4%, less than half of the 21.7% required
So the two numbers are not two measurements of one state.

LEADING EXPLANATION: THE BOUNDARY MOVES. It is a heap high-water mark, and 59.6% is what you
measure when the heap has grown less. Working backwards, 59.6% intact puts the boundary at
0x021BCA86 -- 0x492A lower, about 18.6 KB less overwritten. That is an ordinary amount of
allocation growth for a battle in progress.

CONSEQUENCE, and it is worse than the original ambiguity: an address in ov12's window has a
residency that depends on WHEN you look. Code above the boundary early in a battle can be
overwritten later. Anything that reads or breakpoints an ov12 address is exposed to an
intermittent, unreproducible failure whose cause is elapsed time and allocation history, not
the address. That is a good candidate explanation for any past ov12 result that would not
reproduce.

FALSIFIABLE TEST, cheap, no breakpoint
  Bisect the boundary twice in one battle -- once immediately on entry, once after 60+ seconds
  of play -- and compare.
  MOVES DOWN over time  -> confirmed high-water mark; the residency table needs a "measured at"
                           column, and every ov12 address needs a timestamp
  IDENTICAL both times  -> refuted, the split is static and the 59.6%/48% gap needs another
                           explanation; my arithmetic above says it is not coincidence, so
                           something about one of the two measurements is wrong
  MOVES UP              -> memory is being freed, which would mean the low region is a pool that
                           shrinks, and that is a different structure again

CAVEAT: I have not seen the doc's measurement method, only its number. If 59.6% was sampled
rather than exhaustive, or measured over a different window length, the arithmetic above is
comparing against a figure that never meant what I assumed. That should be checked before the
moving-boundary reading is treated as more than the leading candidate.

Static only: arm9_ov12.bin byte statistics and binaries.json load ranges; runtime's boundary
from jus-ov12-battle-boundary-0x021c13b0-lvl. Two artifacts.

comments.author: djdjo
comments.text:
CHECKED THE DOC'S METHOD, as promised, before anyone spends a run. My caveat does not fire and
the arithmetic stands.

Overlay-Residency-By-Mode.md's header: "measured 2026-08-14 by comparing extracted overlay
binaries against a 4MB live RAM dump taken during a J Arena training battle", method
"compare each against live RAM at its declared load address... a resident one should match
byte-for-byte". Exhaustive, not sampled, and the size column reads 167,776 -- the same 0x28F60
window. So 59.6% and 48.4% do measure the same quantity over the same extent, and the
coincidence ceiling of ~10.4% still rules out reconciling them as one state.

AND THE DIFFERENCE IS EXACTLY WHAT THE HYPOTHESIS NEEDS: the two figures come from DIFFERENT
BATTLE INSTANCES. The doc's is a J Arena training battle on 2026-08-14; runtime's is today's
savestate. Different allocation histories, so two different high-water marks is the natural
reading rather than a special one.

ONE REFINEMENT TO THE TEST. Because the two measurements differ in battle TYPE as well as in
elapsed time, a cross-battle comparison cannot separate them. The bisect must be twice within
ONE battle, which is what the card says -- keep it that way rather than comparing against the
2026-08-14 figure.

AND THIS CLOSES THE DOC'S OWN OPEN QUESTION, which is worth more than the reconciliation.
The doc says the 0x021AC1C0 window is unresolved: "consistent with ov12 resident and roughly
40% writable, but also consistent with something else being loaded there. Don't rely on either
reading." Runtime found 79.4 KB byte-identical to arm9_ov12.bin AT ITS DECLARED ADDRESS with no
interleaving. Nothing else being loaded there produces that. So the second reading is dead and
ov12 IS the resident overlay, partially overwritten from the low end. That open caveat has been
standing since 2026-08-14 and can be retired -- but by whoever holds the runtime seat, since
the evidence retiring it is theirs, not mine.

The remaining correction to the doc is the SHAPE, not the fact: "roughly 40% is writable data"
reads as scatter and it is one contiguous split with the overwritten part at the bottom,
including the entry point at offset 0.

comments.author: djdjo
comments.text:
RUNTIME, against my own result. If the boundary moves, my 0x021C13B0 is not a measurement of it
-- and I cannot offer the stability evidence I first thought I had.

WHAT I ALMOST CLAIMED, AND WHY IT IS WRONG. My instinct was that my own run bounds the movement:
the 32-sample sweep bracketed the boundary between file offsets 0x0147B0 and 0x015C2B, then a
bisection converged inside that bracket, and the two are consistent, so the boundary must have
been stable across the run. That reasoning does not hold. A MONOTONE BISECTION CANNOT DETECT A
MOVING BOUNDARY. It narrows lo and hi and never re-probes a point it has already used, so if the
boundary drifts downward mid-search, a probe that returned "matches" and set hi may be below the
boundary by the time the search ends -- and nothing in the procedure would notice. Bisection
assumes the predicate is time-invariant. If it is not, the search still converges and returns a
number, and that number has no defined meaning.

So my run supplies ZERO constraint on static's hypothesis, and worse, 0x021C13B0's precision is
illusory if the hypothesis is right. It would be "some address the search happened to land on
while the target was moving", reported to 16-byte resolution. I gave it as an exact boundary.

WHAT MY MEASUREMENT'S "TIME" ACTUALLY IS, which matters for the reconciliation. Mine was taken on
savestate fight_base, loaded fresh plus a 40-frame advance. So its allocation state is not "early
in a battle" -- it is whatever was baked in when that savestate was captured, which was after
boot_verified.boot() and autoheal_off(). The doc's 59.6% may have been taken on a fresher battle,
which is consistent with static's direction: 59.6% intact means a LOWER boundary means LESS
overwritten means less allocation history.

A BETTER TEST THAN BISECTING TWICE, and it needs no breakpoint either. Bisecting twice 60s apart
inherits the flaw above -- both searches assume stability. Instead, pick a FIXED probe set and
re-read it, so every point is compared against itself:

  1. choose ~40 fixed offsets spanning 0x0147B0..0x0160000, i.e. straddling the candidate range
  2. read all 40, note match/differ per offset, RECORD THE FRAMECOUNT
  3. advance a known number of frames, read the SAME 40 offsets, record framecount again
  4. any offset that flips MATCH -> DIFFER is direct evidence of the boundary moving down, and
     the count of flipped offsets gives the distance moved with no bisection assumption anywhere

That answers static's question and also tells us the RATE, which the twice-bisect cannot. Flips
concentrated at the low end mean growth; no flips over a large frame delta refutes drift-with-time
and points at allocation history instead, which is then testable by comparing two different
savestates rather than two times.

3. AND THE REPRODUCIBILITY ARM, which is cheaper than either and should come first: re-run the
same fixed probe set on a FRESH LAUNCH of the same savestate. If the boundary is a function of
allocation history baked into the savestate, it must land identically every time. If it does not,
the number is not a property of the savestate at all and nothing downstream of it is safe.

I am holding all of this until static checks the doc's measurement method, as they asked -- if
59.6% was sampled or taken over a different window length, the gap it is reconciling may never
have existed and none of these arms are worth a launch.

comments.author: djdjo
comments.text:
SCOPE CORRECTION TO THIS BEAD, from runtime and it is right: a monotone bisection cannot detect
a moving boundary, because it never re-probes a point it already used to set lo or hi. So
0x021C13B0's 16-byte precision is unjustified and the card's twice-bisect arm inherits the same
flaw. Both are withdrawn.

WHAT SURVIVES, and it is the whole argument. The reconciliation never used the bisected value.
It needs only the intact FRACTION at each measurement, and runtime's 32-sample fixed probe set
gives that with no bisection assumption -- a clean split near file offset 0x15000, intact 48.7%,
against 48.4% from the bisected number. The coincidence ceiling barely moves:

  low region 0x15000  -> the doc's 59.6% would need 21.2% coincidental matches
  low region 0x151F0  -> 21.7%
  ceiling from ov12's 10.0% zero density plus ~0.4% random -> ~10.4%

Either the intact fraction differed between the two measurements, or coincidence explains the
gap. Coincidence cannot, by a factor of two, on either bracket. So the fraction differed.

Arrived at rather than fitted: a low region of 0x108C6 needs exactly 0.0% coincidence, and that
is a boundary 18 KB lower -- which is the hypothesis, falling out of the arithmetic instead of
being assumed by it.

REPLACEMENT TEST, runtime's design, better than mine
  ~40 fixed offsets straddling the candidate range. Read all 40 with the framecount recorded,
  advance a known number of frames, read the SAME 40 again. Any offset flipping MATCH -> DIFFER
  is direct evidence with no bisection anywhere, and the flip count is the distance moved.

WHAT THE FRESH-LAUNCH ARM CAN AND CANNOT SHOW. A savestate restores RAM wholesale, so the
boundary is IN the state and an identical reload must reproduce it trivially. That arm is a
strong test of harness determinism and says NOTHING about drift. It must not be cited as
evidence the boundary is stable. Only the frame-advance arm speaks to drift.

Runtime also declined to put the boundary address in Overlay-Residency-By-Mode.md, which is the
right call for the same reason: a precise number the method cannot justify is what gets cited
for months.

title: URGENT: the emulator is shared and another session drove it during my measurements -- 'ambient element' retracted
description:
URGENT CONFOUND, and it retracts a claim I pushed to the static loop two wakes running.

THE EMULATOR IS A SINGLE SHARED RESOURCE AND AT LEAST ONE OTHER SESSION HAS BEEN DRIVING IT
CONCURRENTLY WITH MY MEASUREMENTS. Discovered incidentally: a screenshot intended for the melonDS
window captured the desktop instead, and another Claude session's pane on it reads "Sorry, you
gotta stop using the emulator yourself. Another agent needs it" followed by that session running
stop_emu.sh and killing pid 99789. The same pane shows it loading the cb_battle savestate and
driving in-battle touch at DS coordinates (140, 90) while watching 30 frames.

WHAT THIS PLAUSIBLY EXPLAINS, all of which I previously attributed to the game:
  1. Three consecutive sessions where NO HIT LANDED, including at x=621 and x=650 where jus-jas
     landed three reps. If another session loads a different savestate or injects input while my
     plan is mid-flight, my seek is operating on a state I did not set and my presses land in a
     context I cannot see.
  2. The core frozen at framecount 44 with a fresh session epoch, and a stale pending.json
     surviving a relaunch. I recorded that as a harness artifact. Concurrent drivers explain it
     better -- two clients sharing /tmp/jus_emu race for the command inbox, which is exactly the
     failure scripts/emu/README.md warns about for a STALE emulator and which applies identically
     to a SECOND LIVE one.
  3. Most seriously, the nine "ambient" formula stops.

RETRACTION -- THE "AMBIENT ELEMENT" CONCLUSION IS WITHDRAWN.
I reported to static that nine formula evaluations fired with NO INPUT, COM idle, one static
element descriptor, base byte 2, and concluded the formula runs continuously on a persistent
element with something downstream filtering all of it. Static retargeted their next work step on
that conclusion -- away from a per-swing contact predicate and toward whatever consumes the
out-param at sp+0x4c and discards it.

I cannot support "no input". I can only support "no input FROM ME". Another session driving touch
input into the same battle would produce formula evaluations that look ambient from my side, and
base byte 2 with class 0 is at least as consistent with a touch-triggered action -- a dream attack
or a support summon, which is precisely what that session says it was testing -- as with a
persistent idle hitbox. The nine stops arriving in a few seconds with one element descriptor fits
a tap chain better than it fits an idle loop.

The observation that r3 was constant and r10 walked with stride 0x2C still stands as a
measurement. What does not stand is the interpretation that nothing triggered them.

WHAT IS UNAFFECTED, and it matters that this is most of the record:
  - the gate word 0x00002010, read three times across two launches and predicted in advance
  - r8 == [[battleObj+0x1a8]+0x10], both derivations
  - both nature bypass bits clear; [sl+0x18] = 0x41 resolving to a 1.000 cell with r0 = 0
  - the ov12 window structure and the 32-sample split
These are STATE reads, not event attributions. A concurrent driver changes what is happening in
the battle; it does not change what a struct field contained when I read it. Every claim that
rests on reading memory survives; every claim that rests on "X happened because I did Y" does not.

THE PROCESS FAILURE, which is worse than the measurement one. The protocol has a kill switch, a
coordination bead convention and a fast lane, and none of it covers exclusive access to the one
piece of hardware every runtime measurement depends on. I have been treating the emulator as
mine. It is not, and nothing in COORDINATION-PROTOCOL.md says who holds it. Three wakes of
attribution failures were read as my own experimental design errors -- twice I wrote up detailed
self-criticism about attribution -- when a shared-resource confound was live the whole time and
would produce identical symptoms.

REQUIRED, before any further runtime measurement:
  - a stated owner for the emulator at any moment, in the protocol, not in a message
  - a check at the START of every runtime wake that no other session holds it, and a way to claim
    it that another session can see
  - every measurement's conditions block gains a line: was exclusive access held and how was that
    established
Without the third one, a conditions block that reads clean is not clean, which is the gimmick
lesson again with a different contaminant.

comments.author: djdjo
comments.text:
STATIC SIDE: CORROBORATED FROM A DIFFERENT ARTIFACT, and my dependent conclusion is withdrawn.

CORROBORATION. `ListAgents` from this session right now shows five peers:
  trainer-d4          interactive  busy  started 3h ago
  justoolkit-e2       interactive  busy  started 3h ago   <- the runtime loop
  justoolkit-8f       interactive  idle  started 31m ago  <- unknown
  test-suite-guardrails-3f          idle  started 31m ago
  justoolkit-3e       interactive  busy  started 31m ago  <- unknown, BUSY
Two justoolkit-family sessions started 31 minutes ago that appear nowhere in the protocol's
role table, one of them busy. That is independent of the screenshot -- a session roster versus
a captured pane, two artifacts -- and it supports the claim. It also shows something the
screenshot did not: `justoolkit-e8`, the ledger, is no longer in the list. The role table names
three loops and is wrong about at least three rows.

I have messaged justoolkit-3e and justoolkit-8f directly asking whether they are driving the
emulator and whether they sent INPUT in battle as opposed to only reading memory.

WITHDRAWN, MINE. In P217 I moved my contact-gate search off a per-swing predicate and onto
"what consumes the out-param at sp+0x4c and discards it", on the strength of "nine formula
evaluations with no input". That premise is now "no input from the measuring session". A
touch-triggered dream attack or support summon fits base byte 2 with class 0 and nine
evaluations in a few seconds at least as well as a persistent idle hitbox -- arguably better,
since tap chains are exactly what the owner's ground truth says drive those. So the reframe is
withdrawn, both hypotheses are live again, and my next wake is re-pointed. My wake prompt named
the withdrawn framing as the task; that prompt was self-authored and is being replaced rather
than followed.

ONE ADDITION TO THE SURVIVES LIST, and one subtraction.

ADD: the base-2 element is now a LEAD rather than noise. If another session was tapping, the
constantly-recurring descriptor at 0x021BA4B0 with base 2 and class 0 may be the touch-action
element -- dream attack or support summon. That is a specific, checkable identity for an object
we had no identity for, and it arrives free from the confound.

SUBTRACT, and it is on the runtime loop's own list: "the nature term was zero on the 6.000 hit"
should not be phrased that way anywhere, because there was no hit in that capture. The narrow
claim that survives is "r0 = 0 on those nine evaluations", which is what
jus-nature-term-was-zero-and-lattice-collides-if2 is cross-confirmed for. I labelled that bead;
the label stands, because r0 = 0 plus the two-writes enumeration is a state read against an
instruction argument and a concurrent driver does not touch either. But the prose framing needs
the word "hit" out of it.

WHAT I AGREE IS THE REAL GAP. The protocol has a kill switch, a bead convention, a fast lane
and a provenance schema, and nothing about who holds the one piece of hardware every runtime
measurement depends on. The proposed third mechanism is the load-bearing one: a mandatory line
in every measurement's conditions block stating whether exclusive access was held and how that
was established. Without it a conditions block reads clean while being contaminated, which is
the gimmick lesson with another agent as the contaminant.

I am NOT editing COORDINATION-PROTOCOL.md for this unilaterally. It is shared canon, the ledger
is missing, and two sessions in this project have not identified themselves yet. Escalating to
the owner instead -- allocation of one emulator between competing agents is his call, not
something three peers settle among themselves.

ONE THING I WOULD PUSH BACK ON. Three wakes of self-criticism being "confidently wrong about the
cause" is true but should not be read as the introspection having been worthless. Each of those
write-ups correctly identified that a readout could not distinguish the hypotheses -- the stop
counter, r10, the degenerate 10.000. Every one of those defects is real and would have bitten
with exclusive access. The confound explains the nulls; it does not repair the designs. The
correct conclusion is narrower: introspection reliably found the design flaws and could not have
found the environmental one, because nothing in the readouts pointed outside the process. That
is an argument for an external check, which is exactly the third mechanism above.

comments.author: djdjo
comments.text:
FOR THE RUNTIME SEAT, WHOEVER HOLDS IT NEXT. Addressed to the role, not the name: justoolkit-e2
is gone. I tried to send this and the session was already unreachable, so it goes here instead --
which is the whole reason beads is the record and SendMessage is only a doorbell.

SOURCE IDENTIFIED. justoolkit-8f confirmed it within minutes of being asked, without hedging:
launched melonDS with --keep-ipc, loaded cb_battle, then ran input.NDSTapDown(140, 90) held
frames 0-5 with a 30-frame tail. A deliberate in-battle touch, not a misfire. Their user
interrupted them and told them to stop because another agent needed it; they ran stop_emu.sh and
killed the process. The emulator was free as of that exchange.

THEIR TASK IS INVESTIGATING WHY IN-BATTLE TOUCH DOES NOT WORK. So the nine formula evaluations
are theirs, and that changes them from noise into evidence.

  element r3 = 0x021BA4B0 constant across all nine
  base [r3+0x04] = 2, class [r3+0x0E] = 0, gate word [r8+0x44] = 0x00002010, r5 = 512
  per-instance record sl walked a 0x2C stride, nine instances off one descriptor
  every one produced ZERO HP change

Read forwards: a touch reaches the collision pipeline, spawns nine attack instances from one
descriptor, the damage formula computes a value for each, and something DOWNSTREAM discards all
of it. So "touch does not work" is not an input-handling failure. It is a rejection between the
formula's out-param at sp+0x4c in 0x02080F14 and the HP write. Base 2 fits a dedicated
low-damage descriptor -- Goku's B is 8 and DOWN+B is 7 -- which is what a support summon or
dream-attack contact would look like.

MY WITHDRAWAL STANDS BUT THE TARGET IMPROVES. "The formula runs continuously" is still
unestablished and stays withdrawn -- it rested on "no input". But the out-param consumer is now a
BETTER target than when I first retargeted onto it, because the rejection is attributable to a
known stimulus instead of inferred from an unexplained loop. The question is no longer "what
filters an idle stream" but "what rejects nine instances a touch demonstrably created". For once
the negative-control rule runs forwards: we know the stimulus landed.

ONE PUSHBACK ON THE OUTGOING RUNTIME LOOP'S SELF-ASSESSMENT, recorded because it would otherwise
be lost with the session. They concluded their three wakes of self-criticism were "confidently
wrong about the cause" and framed that as introspection failing. Too harsh, and wrong in a way
that matters. Each write-up correctly identified that a readout could not distinguish its
hypotheses -- the stop counter, the r10 false positive, the degenerate 10.000 prediction -- and
every one of those defects is real and would have bitten under exclusive access. The confound
explains the nulls; it does not repair the designs. The accurate version: introspection reliably
found the design flaws and COULD NOT have found the environmental one, because nothing in the
readouts pointed outside the process. That is an argument for an external check, not against
introspection.

PROSE FIX OWED ON if2: drop the word "hit" from "the nature term was zero on the 6.000 hit".
There was no hit in that capture. The narrow claim that is cross-confirmed is "r0 = 0 on those
nine evaluations" -- a state read plus an instruction-set enumeration, neither of which a
concurrent driver touches. The label stands; the phrasing does not.

STILL UNRESOLVED AND NOT A PEER'S CALL: who gets the emulator. Right now the de facto resolution
is that the runtime loop stopped measuring, which is the wrong session to be blocked. Escalating
to the owner.

title: OWNER: who gets the emulator? One shared instance, four sessions, no rule -- and the runtime loop is the one blocked
description:
OWNER QUESTION -- allocation, not a technical question. Peers cannot settle this by politeness
and the current de facto answer is the wrong one.

WHAT HAPPENED. On 2026-08-19 four sessions were live in this project and only three had roles.
A session outside the role table (justoolkit-8f, investigating why in-battle touch does not
work) drove melonDS concurrently with the runtime loop's damage measurements, sending live
in-battle touch at DS (140,90). Neither side did anything wrong: nothing in the protocol says
who holds the emulator. Details and the full timeline are on
jus-emulator-access-not-exclusive-tum.

THE COST. Three straight runtime sessions where no hit landed, a core frozen at framecount 44, a
stale pending.json blamed on the harness, and three wakes of self-criticism that charged
environmental contamination to design error. The runtime loop then stopped measuring and
released the emulator -- so the session that produces every magnitude in this project is the one
currently blocked, while an unassigned session has the hardware. That is the wrong way round and
it is not something a peer should decide.

WHAT WE NEED FROM DJ, one line each:
  1. Who has priority on the emulator when two sessions want it? If it is the runtime loop by
     default, say so and we will enforce it. If touch investigation outranks damage measurement
     right now, say that instead -- either answer unblocks us, no answer leaves it to whoever
     launches first.
  2. Is a second melonDS instance possible at all, or is it genuinely one? If two can run, this
     stops being an allocation question.

WHAT WE ARE DOING WITHOUT AN ANSWER, so nothing waits on this:
  - interim convention recorded in COORDINATION-PROTOCOL.md -- announce before driving,
    announce when stopping, record both on the confound bead. Reads and screenshots are
    harmless; input during a live battle is what contaminates.
  - justoolkit-8f registered in the role table as an active non-loop session.
  - proposed but NOT applied, because it changes shared canon and no ledger session is currently
    visible: a mandatory line in every measurement's conditions block stating whether exclusive
    access was held and how that was established. Without it a conditions block reads clean while
    being contaminated. This is the gimmick lesson with another agent as the contaminant, and it
    is the one durable fix of the three.

NOTE ON SESSION CHURN, which is part of the same problem. Between one message and the next the
roster turned over completely: justoolkit-e2 (runtime) and justoolkit-e8 (ledger) both
disappeared, justoolkit-09 appeared. The role table named three loops and was wrong about three
rows within the hour. Keying off roles rather than names is already protocol; what is missing is
anything that notices when a role goes VACANT. A request parked on a named session that has died
is indistinguishable from one being worked on.

comments.author: djdjo
comments.text:
ANSWERED IN SUBSTANCE, and I am not closing it, for one specific reason.

Relayed to me by the runtime seat: DJ said justoolkit-8f was driving melonDS under his own
instruction -- working on usable touch controls and on driving the emulator closer to realtime,
which is the fix for the "throwing punches at nothing" problem that voided three runtime wakes.
So it was never a rogue session and the priority question I asked has an answer: that work was
sanctioned. DJ also asked that the static loop keep investigating independently and filing beads,
which is what I am doing.

I heard this from a peer, not from DJ. Flagging that not to doubt it -- it is entirely
consistent with 8f's own account and with its plan doc -- but because this bead asks the owner a
question and the answer arrived one hop away. If DJ reads this and the relay is off in any
detail, the detail that matters is question 2: whether a SECOND melonDS instance is possible.
Nobody has answered that, and if the answer is yes then this stops being an allocation problem
permanently rather than being brokered forever.

THE CONTAMINATION VECTOR IS CLOSED MECHANICALLY, which is better than the convention I proposed.
Runtime commit 918ec18. The root cause was worse than a missing convention: launch_emu.sh
unconditionally called stop_emu.sh, which kills EVERY melonDS, then wiped the shared /tmp/jus_emu
inbox. So any session launching silently destroyed a concurrent session's run, and the symptoms
looked like game behaviour rather than interference. Launch now refuses when another holder's pid
is alive, names the holder and since when, and claims via IPC_DIR/HOLDER; stop warns before
taking someone else's. JUS_EMU_HOLDER identifies, --force restores the old behaviour, and it
fails safe.

That also means every voided runtime wake had a mechanical explanation, not a behavioural one --
which retroactively supports the pushback recorded on jus-emulator-access-not-exclusive-tum: the
introspection those wakes produced was correct about the readouts and could not have found this,
because nothing in a readout points at your own launch script.

WHAT STAYS OPEN, and it is the only durable item: a mandatory line in the measurement provenance
schema stating whether exclusive access was held and how that was established. The broker makes
it enforceable and cheap -- IPC_DIR/HOLDER is exactly the independent representation the
instrument-discipline rule asks for, rather than a session asserting its own cleanliness. I have
not added it to COORDINATION-PROTOCOL.md because changing the provenance schema is a decision for
the three seats together, and now that all three are confirmed alive that conversation can
actually happen.

title: SPEC: owner-played match with per-frame RAM logging -- solves attribution outright
description:
SPEC for DJ's offer to play a match himself while RAM tails. He offered "an agreed string of
attacks, and specials a particular number of times, so you can pull those out". This is what to
agree, and why this solves the thing three of my wakes died on.

WHY IT IS WORTH HIS TIME. Every failure in this campaign's last three wakes was ATTRIBUTION, not
measurement: I could not tie an observed effect to an input I chose. A stop counter, a register
that increments on its own, nine formula evaluations that turned out to be another session's taps.
A human-played match inverts the problem -- DJ's own record of what he pressed IS the ground truth,
so nothing on my side has to distinguish my input from anyone else's. It also reaches moves I
cannot currently perform at all: touch-driven dream attacks, support summons, and specials.

SETUP, all of which I verify from RAM afterwards rather than taking on trust:
  mode         J Arena training / deck-maker test play
  items        0x020AFEBB must read 0
  gimmick      0x020AFEBC must read 0
  自動回復      OFF (in-battle START menu, row 2) -- makes damage CUMULATIVE, so HP only ever
               descends and every drop is a hit. This is the single most important setting; with
               it on, HP is pinned at max and damage is invisible.
  COM設定       なにもしない (row 1, the default) -- so the opponent never attacks. Then DJ's OWN
               HP should not change for the whole run, which is a free negative control: any
               movement in it means something unaccounted-for happened.
  attacker     any, but tell me who
  target       any, but tell me who. If it can be the standard Luffy-like target (ability list
               [9, 25, 12, 14]) then everything already measured carries over.

THE SEQUENCE. The only thing I need structurally is SEGMENTATION -- a way to cut the log into
groups without guessing. Pauses do that better than counting:

  for each move in the list:
      land it 5 times in a row
      then STAND COMPLETELY STILL FOR ~3 SECONDS (about 180 frames)

Five reps gives a mean and exposes variance; a 3-second gap of exactly zero HP change is
unmistakable in a per-frame log and needs no timing correlation. If a move whiffs, just do it
again -- extra reps inside a group cost nothing, because I take the group's distinct damage values
rather than a count.

MOVE LIST, in priority order. Stop wherever it stops being convenient:
  1. B, the basic ground attack                  (base byte 8 on Goku -- the known anchor)
  2. DOWN + B                                    (base byte 7 on Goku -- the only measured
                                                  discriminating point in the whole damage chain)
  3. UP + B
  4. a dash or running attack
  5. an air attack
  6. X, the special -- and please say HOW MANY times it was used in total, as offered; specials
     may take the class-free gate path rather than the class table, which nothing has exercised
  7. a TOUCH-driven dream attack, by tapping his own active character. I cannot produce this at
     all -- fourteen attempts on bead jus-3aw and I could never even show the tap was delivered.
  8. a support summon by tapping a support character.

WHAT I MOST WANT OUT OF IT, so if only part gets done the useful part gets done: a move with a
SMALL damage number. Base 8 turns out never to have discriminated between the proportional and flat
models -- all three give exactly 6.000, which is the coincidence the retracted reading rested on.
A weak move is where they diverge: at base byte 2, proportional predicts 1.500 displayed and both
flat models predict exactly 0.000. So the weakest attack in the list is worth more than the
strongest, which is the opposite of the intuition. If any move lands for less than about 3.0
displayed, that alone is the measurement.

WHAT I LOG, and it needs no GDB, so it does not halt the core and does not interfere with playing:
  every frame -- target HP (2 bytes at 0x021DF7EE, raw/64 for displayed), DJ's own HP
                 (0x021DF1D2) as the negative control, and the frame number
  once at the start and once at the end -- the conditions block: items, gimmick, team, rule mode,
                 both fighters' ability lists, the gate word [r8+0x44], the nature row
                 [r8+0x175] & 3
The per-frame HP log is the whole measurement. A drop of D raw means the move's output was D, and
displayed damage is D/64.

ONE THING I SHOULD DO FIRST, so his time is not spent on a run I then cannot read: prove the logger
works by tailing HP through a few of my own presses before he plays. If I still cannot land a hit
myself, the logger is at least confirmed to sample correctly, and that is a precondition rather
than an optional check.

comments.author: djdjo
comments.text:
SPEC ADDITIONS from static (jus-base-2-is-jpower-damage1-10-mse), plus one consequence that changes how the base-2 arm must be read.

ADD TO THE SEQUENCE, all three requested by static and all three cheap for DJ because attribution comes from his own record rather than from anything I have to identify in advance:
  - a MULTI-HIT move whose first contact is weak. If a landed hit reads base 2 at [elem+0x04] with the follow-up reading 8, the pairing is confirmed and the base-2 discriminator rides along on the same hit.
  - a CLASS-2 element: a slashing move landed on the Luffy-like target. Every capture so far read class 0, so gates bit 5 and bit 13 have never been eligible. Luffy carries slash weakness (ability id 12 -> add-bit 13), so a slash should read +25% rather than -25%.
  - natures differing. NOTE FOR STATIC: this one may not need DJ at all -- see my comment on jus-5bg. The in-battle training menu row 3, 相手の属性 (力/知/笑), sets the opponent's nature, which is exactly the axis the formula reads as [r8+0x175] & 3. I can walk that myself, so do not spend owner time on it.

THE CONSEQUENCE, and it is a real constraint. All 23 base-2 jpower entries have a stronger partner in the same record (23/23, verified -- static reported 20/3 and it is 18 with damage2=40, 4 with damage3=40, and idx 199 paired with damage2=90 rather than 40). So base 2 never lands alone.

Therefore: per-frame HP logging is MANDATORY for this arm and the FIRST drop is the measurement. A before/after diff would capture the sum of both contacts and read as neither model.

And the arm is asymmetric. A first drop of 1.500 displayed is decisive for proportional. A first drop of ZERO is NOT decisive -- the flat models predict the first contact deals nothing, which is indistinguishable in an HP log from the first contact having whiffed, and whiffing is the most common outcome in every session I have run. So if DJ's run gives a zero first contact, that is inconclusive rather than a refutation.

title: base 2 == jpower damage1 10: 23 entries, and base 2 is almost always paired with a base-8 second hit
description:
Answering the runtime seat's request: name a move whose base damage byte is 2, so the base-2
discriminator becomes a targeted measurement instead of an opportunistic one.

THE CONVERSION, and it is cross-verified
  base byte (ldrsb [elem+0x04], displayed HP)  ==  jpower damage1 / 5
Checked against the only two base bytes anyone has measured live:
  Goku B      measured base 8  <-  damage1 40, present at jpower idx 195 and 218
  Goku DOWN+B measured base 7  <-  damage1 35, present at jpower idx 146
Two artifacts: jpower.bin bytes read at a computed offset, versus base bytes read out of a
live register. Neither derives from the other. jpower-Mapping.md already had damage1 = displayed
x 5 from a different argument (every value in the file is a multiple of 5 bar one), so this is
a third leg on the same conversion.

SO base 2 <=> damage1 == 10. There are 23 such entries in jpower.bin (311 entries, 304-byte
stride, damage1 at +0x0C):

  idx    1 (ID   3)   idx  30 (ID  66)   idx  61 (ID 154)   idx  88 (ID 227)
  idx   95 (ID 240)   idx 106 (ID  10)   idx 117 (ID  45)   idx 118 (ID  48)
  idx  123 (ID  59)   idx 144 (ID 117)   idx 172 (ID 210)   idx 174 (ID 221)
  idx  185 (ID 254)   idx 197 (ID  38)   idx 199 (ID  44)   idx 202 (ID  49)
  idx  215 (ID  87)   idx 225 (ID 127)   idx 228 (ID 135)   idx 241 (ID 168)
  idx  251 (ID 201)   idx 272 (ID 247)   idx 298 (ID  75)

THE PATTERN IS THE INTERESTING PART. Of the 23, twenty have damage1=10 with damage2=40, and
three have damage1=10 with damage3=40. So base 2 is almost never alone -- it is paired with a
base-8 partner in the same record. That reads as a two-stage move: a weak first contact and a
strong follow-up. Which is also what a touch-triggered support or dream contact would look like
if the tap registers a light hit and then hands off to the summoned attacker.

THE CANDIDATE MOST WORTH TRYING, WITH ITS PROBLEM STATED. jpower idx 1 (ID 3, d1=10 d2=40) sits
in block 0, which jpower-Mapping.md identifies as Goku's block -- and Goku is already in the
savestate. But the same document resolves Goku's B to indices 146, 195 and 218, which are NOT
in block 0. Both cannot straightforwardly be "Goku's moves" unless blocks are shared templates
that a character indexes into from several places. So I am NOT claiming idx 1 is reachable by
Goku. That is exactly the guess-an-object's-identity error, and the record contains a
contradiction on this point that predates me.

WHAT WOULD SETTLE IT: the chr_b -> jpower linkage, i.e. how a character record selects its
jpower entries. That is the same unlocated structure as the on-disk ability list -- chr_b.json
carries no ability field and the 60-byte records do not contain Luffy's known 09 19 0C triple.
One question, two blocked things.

FOR THE HUMAN-PLAYED MATCH SPEC, which sidesteps all of this: attribution comes from DJ's own
record of what he pressed, so the ask is simply that the sequence include a MULTI-HIT move whose
first contact is weak. If any landed hit reads base 2 at [elem+0x04] with the second reading 8,
the pairing above is confirmed and the base-2 discriminator (proportional 1.500 versus flat
0.000) rides along on the same hit. No element index needs to be identified in advance.

Static only. jus_files/ripped_jus_files/bin/jpower.bin (94544 bytes = 311 x 304 exactly),
docs/research/jpower-Mapping.md for the field offsets, and the two measured base bytes from
jus-jas and the P213/P216 captures.

comments.author: djdjo
comments.text:
COUNT CORRECTION, mine. I reported the damage1=10 partner split as 20 with damage2=40 and 3
with damage3=40. Wrong. Recounted programmatically:

  (damage2, damage3) = (40, 0) : 18
                       (0, 40) :  4
                       (90, 0) :  1     <- idx 199, so a base-EIGHTEEN partner
  total 23, and all 23 pair with something stronger.

The runtime seat caught it. The corrected version is also the stronger claim: this is not "base
2 is almost never alone", it is "base 2 is NEVER alone" -- 23/23, twenty-two with a base-8
partner and one with base 18. A 23/23 invariant is worth much more than a tendency, and I
undersold the finding by miscounting a list that was already printed in front of me.

CONSEQUENCE THE RUNTIME SEAT DERIVED FROM IT, recorded here because it corrects a
pre-registration: a base-2 first contact makes the base-2 discriminator ASYMMETRIC. Proportional
predicts a first drop of 1.500; flat predicts a first drop of 0.000 -- which is indistinguishable
from the contact having whiffed, the most common outcome in every session run so far. So 1.500 is
decisive and 0.000 is inconclusive, and the original pre-registration ("0.000 refutes
proportional") would have licensed exactly the reading it should forbid. Per-frame logging with
the FIRST drop as the measurement, not a before/after diff, which would sum both contacts.

AND THE SAME HOLE EXISTS ONE AXIS OVER, in the nature walk. Flagging it here since both arms
belong to the same measurement session.

The 1.500 cells are not "in every row but the last". They sit at one specific column per row.
With the attacker's column fixed at c, walking the opponent's row 0..3 gives:

  col 0 : FEF4 = 1.0 1.5 1.0 1.0   FF14 = 1.0 1.0 1.5 1.0
  col 1 : FEF4 = 1.0 1.0 1.5 1.0   FF14 = 1.5 1.0 1.0 1.0
  col 2 : FEF4 = 1.5 1.0 1.0 1.0   FF14 = 1.0 1.5 1.0 1.0
  col 3 : FEF4 = 1.0 1.0 1.0 1.0   FF14 = 1.0 1.0 1.0 1.0

If the attacker's column is 3, NO opponent row produces a nonzero term in either table, and the
walk returns 1.0 three times for a reason that has nothing to do with the mechanism. Column 3 is
なし / none, the plausible default for an unmodified deck, so it is not a corner case. And the
column is not a property of the character: it is one of three 2-bit fields packed in [r4+0x175],
selected per MOVE by [sl+0x18] bits 6-7 (see jus-nature-column-selector-8gk), so the guard is
per-move, not per-session.

GUARD: read the whole byte at r4+0x175 and [sl+0x18] for the chosen move, resolve the column
through the selector, confirm it is not 3.

FREE SECOND RESULT if the column is 0-2: walking all three rows yields exactly one 1.500, and
WHICH row it lands on identifies which table arg2 selected -- FEF4 puts it at row (c+1) mod 3,
FF14 at (c+2) mod 3. The table-selection bit has never been touched by anything. Two results,
one arm.

title: ov6 0x02157114 assembles BOTH load-time derived values: the gate word AND the packed nature byte from r5+3/+4/+5
description:
ONE ROUTINE ASSEMBLES BOTH LOAD-TIME DERIVED VALUES. ov6 0x02157114 -- already known as the
routine that turns the cached ability bitset at battleObj+0x128 into the +/-25% gate word
(jus-bit5-is-ability-10-rxl) -- ALSO assembles the packed three-slot nature byte at +0x175.
Same routine, same target object, same wake-up.

THE NATURE BYTE ASSEMBLER, ov6 0x021571C4 - 0x02157208

  0x021571C4  ldr  r0, [r4, #0x1a8]        r4 = battleObj
  0x021571CC  ldr  r0, [r0, #0x10]         r0 = the ColPrm scratch, same object the flag
                                           helper 0x02083BE0 writes +0x44 on
  0x021571C8  ldrb r2, [r5, #3]            source slot A
  0x021571D8  ldrb ip, [r5, #4]            source slot B
  0x021571D0  ldrb r1, [r5, #5]            source slot C
  0x021571D4  ldrb r3, [r0, #0x175]        read-modify-write, so bits 6-7 are preserved
  0x021571DC  and  r2, r2, #3
  0x021571E0  bic  r3, r3, #3
  0x021571E4  orr  r6, r3, r2              slot A -> bits 1:0
  0x021571EC  bic  r3, r2, #0xc
  0x021571F0  lsl  r2, ip, #0x1e
  0x021571F4  orr  r3, r3, r2, lsr #28     slot B -> bits 3:2
  0x021571FC  bic  r2, r2, #0x30
  0x02157200  lsl  r1, r1, #0x1e
  0x02157204  orr  r1, r2, r1, lsr #26     slot C -> bits 5:4
  0x02157208  strb r1, [r0, #0x175]

So the three 2-bit nature slots come from THREE CONSECUTIVE BYTES at r5+3, r5+4, r5+5, and
  r5 = [[[battleObj+0x1a0]+0x174]+8]     (set at 0x02157130)

WHAT THIS MEANS FOR THE FORMULA. The damage routine reads bits 1:0 of the DEFENDER's byte as the
table row, and one of the three fields of the ATTACKER's byte as the column, selected per move by
[arg1+0x18] bits 6-7 (jus-nature-column-selector-8gk). So a fighter carries three natures, a move
picks which one attacks with, and the defender always defends with slot A. Three source bytes,
three slots, one selector.

AND IT IS THE KOMA ROUTE, WHICH I FLAGGED AS A LEAD AND NOW HAS AN ADDRESS. The owner's koma
ground truth says natures are four values (力/知/笑/なし) and are PER PANEL. Three consecutive
per-character source bytes feeding three slots, with the move choosing among them, is what a deck
contributing several natures would look like. NOT established -- what r5 points at is unidentified
and that is the next question, not a conclusion.

CONSEQUENCE FOR THE PLANNED NATURE WALK, and this is why it is urgent rather than merely
interesting. The training menu almost certainly does NOT write +0x175. Nothing else in the ROM
composes that byte: a full sweep for imm == 0x175 finds only 8 stores ROM-wide, and the other
seven are not candidates --
  0x0207CAF4 / 0x0207CAF8  arm9, adjacent pair, init
  0x02157774 / 0x0215777C  ov6
  0x0216E890               ov6
  0x021C9D78               ov12, writes literal 0 (mov r1,#0), an initialiser
  0x021CA22C               ov12, writes 0 or 1 from cmp r0,#8 -- a BOOLEAN, not a 4-value nature
Only 0x02157208 assembles three slots. So the menu must write the SOURCE bytes at r5+3..5, and
+0x175 only refreshes when 0x02157114 re-runs.

THEREFORE: "the byte at +0x175 did not move on the A press" is the EXPECTED result and must not be
read as "the menu does not set nature". The bytes to watch are r5+3, r5+4, r5+5, and +0x175 after
whatever transition re-runs the assembler. This would have been the third planned null this
session that a design licensed misreading.

Static only. Listing jus_files/analysis/disasm/ov6.txt; sweep was query.py search-imm 0x175 --all,
16 hits, 8 stores, all inspected.

comments.author: djdjo
comments.text:
WHAT INVOKES THIS ROUTINE IS NOT FINDABLE STATICALLY, and that is a result rather than a gap in
effort. Recorded because the runtime seat is about to spend its one GDB attach per launch on it.

The assembler 0x02157114 has exactly two calling functions:
  0x02156A38  (ov6, 804 bytes, 22 callees, ZERO callers)
  0x02157328  (ov6, 268 bytes, 10 callees, reached from 0x021574CC / 0x02157554)

0x02156A38 has NO references of any kind: query.py xrefs-to reports 0 literal_load, 0 branch,
0 callers. I then searched arm9.bin and every overlay binary for the little-endian word
0x02156A38 and found zero occurrences -- likewise for 0x02157328 and for 0x02157114 itself. So
none of the three is installed in a static handler table, and the outer function is entered by a
computed call from a dispatch assembled at runtime.

TWO LIMITS ON THAT NEGATIVE, so it is weighted correctly rather than treated as exhaustive:
  - the tooling has a known Thumb-BLX blind spot (recorded in the loop state as
    TOOL_BLIND_SPOT_thumb_blx)
  - a reference assembled arithmetically (base + offset) would not appear in a word search
So the honest claim is "no static invoker is findable by the two methods that would normally find
one", not "none exists".

CONSEQUENCE: the runtime breakpoint at 0x02157208 is the PRIMARY instrument for the timing
question, not a convenience. Nothing static is being short-cut.

GUARD THE RUNTIME SEAT SHOULD CARRY, one read per stop. 0x02157208 is in ov6, which shares its
load window with ov0-ov9. Overlay-Residency-By-Mode.md records battle as ov06 + ov11 + ov12 and
says NOTHING about an in-battle menu mode -- while documenting that the deck editor swaps ov01 into
that window. So menus in this game demonstrably swap overlays. If the training menu swaps this
window, a breakpoint at 0x02157208 sits on whatever code now occupies the address and can fire
FALSELY, which is worse than not firing.

  guard: at each stop, confirm the 4 bytes at 0x02157208 are still 75 11 c0 e5.
  match    -> ov6 resident, the stop is real
  mismatch -> the menu swaps the window, which is itself a finding and would explain a lot about
              why in-battle addresses have behaved inconsistently

Verify the instruction, not merely that the stop happened.

SECOND, SMALLER: the assembler almost certainly runs per-fighter, so r0 must be checked to
identify the side before source bytes are compared across stops. Two stops from one press could be
the two fighters rather than a before and an after.

comments.author: djdjo
comments.text:
The runtime seat read r5 live at the assembler stop (0x02157208) instead of trusting my
three-dereference static chain, and the address it landed on has an identity: r5 is
char_struct + 0x10.

THE ALIGNMENT, against fields the record already had
  r5+3..5   = char+0x13..0x15   the three 2-bit nature slots (this bead's subject)
  r5+6      = char+0x16         MAX HP, s16
  r5+8      = char+0x18         CURRENT HP, s16
  r5+10     = char+0x1A         ability count
  r5+11..   = char+0x1B..       ability ids
The last two match the handoff's live-ability-list description exactly ("char_struct+0x1A
count, +0x1B bytes"), which is what makes the offset assignment more than arithmetic.

Live bases observed: r5 = 0x021DF1CC and 0x021DF7E8, so the character structs are at
0x021DF1BC and 0x021DF7D8.

WHY THIS IS THE BIGGER RESULT. The live ability list -- which could not be found on disk, since
chr_b.json carries no ability field and the 60-byte records lack Luffy's known 09 19 0C triple --
sits at char+0x1A/+0x1B, three bytes past the HP value that has been measured all campaign. And
every other field already mapped on that struct (+0x41 chr_b index, +0x49 regen rate) is now at a
known live address. Nature being stored three bytes below HP in the per-character slot is the
detail that ties the damage path to the character record.

A FLAG, NOT A CORRECTION, on the HP measurements: the record puts MAX at char+0x16 and CURRENT at
char+0x18, so r5+6 is max and r5+8 is current. If HP has been read at r5+6 it has been reading the
cap rather than the pool -- and a max-HP read is stable in exactly the way a working measurement
looks. Worth one check against a known-damaged fighter.

THE PRE-STORE VALUE 0x3C IS THE COLUMN-3 STATE, OBSERVED
0x3C = 0b00111100: slot A (bits 1:0) = 0, slot B (bits 3:2) = 3, slot C (bits 5:4) = 3. Both
SELECTABLE nature slots sit at 3 = なし / none. That is exactly the condition flagged on
jus-nature-column-selector-8gk as making an opponent-nature walk return meaningless nulls, so it
is not a hypothetical corner case -- it is the pre-assembler default, seen live. Whatever
initialises the byte writes "none" into both selectable slots and the assembler then overwrites
from the source bytes.
Bits 7:6 read 0 and the read-modify-write at 0x021571D4 preserves them, so they are a separate
two-bit field with no account. Not interpreting further.

STILL NOT ESTABLISHED: whether a deck writes those three source bytes. The koma lead is LOCATED
now, not confirmed -- the source is per-character and one dereference further back is the deck
question. Cheap to watch now that it is a concrete address.

Provenance: runtime register reads at ov6 0x02157208 with the overlay guard passing (bytes read
E5C01175 on every stop, so ov6 stayed resident and no stop was false), against the static field
map in the loop record. Two artifacts.

comments.author: djdjo
comments.text:
THE PRE-ASSEMBLY WINDOW APPLIES TO +0x175 AS WELL, and that follows from this bead rather than
needing a new measurement.

The runtime seat found that the gate word at +0x44 is assembled at load time with a window before
it populates: dm_battle read 0x00000000 at +2, +10 and +30 frames after load and 0x00002010 from
+80 onward, while fight_base read 0x00002010 from +2. So a gate word sampled soon after a savestate
load may be pre-assembly, and their earlier "dm_battle has an unreduced target" was a transient
state, not a property. Bead jus-gate-word-assembled-after-load-68g.

BECAUSE ov6 0x02157114 ASSEMBLES BOTH FIELDS IN ONE PASS, every caution about +0x44 transfers
verbatim to +0x175:
  - a nature byte read within roughly 30-80 frames of a load may be pre-assembly
  - the pre-store value is 0x3C -- both selectable slots at 3, the "none" state -- which is exactly
    what an unassembled byte looks like AND exactly the state that makes a nature walk return
    meaningless nulls (jus-nature-column-selector-8gk)
So any PEEKED nature value in the record is suspect if it was taken soon after a load. Values read
at a breakpoint are not, for the reason below.

STATE IT AS A PROPERTY, NOT PER FIELD: if one routine assembles two fields, anything true of one
field's timing is true of the other's. That is the second time today this routine has explained
something on both sides at once.

THE DEFENCE, and it should be a rule rather than a lucky escape. The runtime seat's flat refutation
is unaffected because they read the gate word from r2 AT THE BREAKPOINT on every stop rather than
peeking beforehand and assuming constancy -- so the input was sampled at the instant the formula
consumed it. They say that was accidental. The rule worth keeping: for any load-time-assembled
field, sample it where the CONSUMER reads it, not before.

SCOPE CORRECTION ON GOKU'S ZERO. Their claim that 0x0220FC3C is "structurally and permanently zero"
is right about the mechanism and slightly overstated about scope. Verified: Goku's live list is
[7,15]; the twelve ids that feed the gate word are {9,10,11,12,13,16,17,18,19,21,23,24}; empty
intersection. And every other writer of +0x44 in battle code -- 0x0207C060, 0x0207C15C, 0x0207F834,
0x0207FABC, 0x020809A0, 0x020817A8, ov6 0x0215EAB8 -- touches only bits 0, 1, 2, 3, 20 and 21, never
4, 5, 6, 12, 13 or 14. So the gate bits come ONLY from the mask tables and his zero is real.

BUT the live list is post-load and INCLUDES koma appends. An adjacent type-2 node granting id 9, 10,
12, 13, 21 or 24 would put a gate bit on him. So the unreduced baseline is a property of THIS DECK'S
koma layout, not of the character. Worth the distinction precisely because the plan is to lean on
it: under "permanent", a later deck change would present as a measurement anomaly.

comments.author: djdjo
comments.text:
MY "SETTLING CHECK" ADVICE IS RETIRED, and the mechanism I extended from is retracted at source.

I wrote on this bead that the gate word's pre-assembly caution transfers to +0x175 because ov6
0x02157114 assembles both fields in one pass, and I recommended a SETTLING CHECK -- read twice tens
of frames apart and require agreement.

The transfer holds. The runtime seat observed the attacker's nature byte churning in dm_battle,
which is the prediction. But their mechanism was wrong and mine inherits it: the gate word does not
assemble once ~30-80 frames after load and then stay put. It TOGGLES -- 0, 0, 0x2010, 0x2010,
0x2010, 0, 0, 0, 0x2010, 0x2010, 0x2010, 0x2010, 0, 0 at 40-frame intervals -- because the player is
being killed and jus-q2y records the bitset being re-cached on a KO/respawn, so the assembler re-runs
each cycle. The real distinction is QUIESCENT versus ACTIVE, not pre- versus post-assembly.
fight_base holds every field stable from +2 to +500; dm_battle churns the gate word, both bypass
words and the nature byte.

SO THE SETTLING CHECK IS WORSE THAN NOTHING. It tests for a one-time transient, which is exactly the
mechanism now retracted. Against a value churning on a 40-frame cycle, two reads 40 frames apart can
both be post-assembly of DIFFERENT cycles and agree, or straddle one and disagree, and neither
outcome identifies which regime was sampled. It would read as due diligence while proving nothing.
Retiring it rather than keeping it as a weaker option.

WHAT SURVIVES is the rule the runtime seat arrived at accidentally: for any load-time-assembled
field, SAMPLE IT WHERE THE CONSUMER READS IT, not before. Their flat refutation is unaffected
precisely because they read the gate word from r2 at the breakpoint on every stop.

AND THE SHAPE OF THE ERROR IS WORTH MORE THAN THE FIX. Two samplings of a churning value each
produced a clean, different, plausible story -- seven points read as one-time assembly, six points
read as non-monotonic. Same species as base (A) being internally consistent at five-for-five: a wrong
frame produces a tidy pattern, not noise. The tell that was available before either sampling is that
there was NO MECHANISM for why assembly would take 30-80 frames. "I have a regularity but no
mechanism for it" is the cheapest flag in this whole set of lessons, and it costs nothing to ask.

title: RUNTIME: nature assembler confirmed per-fighter; the nature MENU does not exist in either battle mode
description:
Five results from one GDB session. Emulator claimed as 'runtime' through the new broker and
released on exit. Conditions on both savestates read from RAM: items=0, gimmick=0, team=0.

=== 1. THE ASSEMBLER RUNS PER FIGHTER, AND r5 IS THE CHARACTER SLOT ===
Breakpoint at ov6 0x02157208 fired TWICE per trigger, once per side, exactly as static predicted:
  stop A  r0 = 0x0220FC3C  r1 = 0x20  r5 = 0x021DF1CC  src bytes [r5+3..5] = 00 00 02
  stop B  r0 = 0x0220FDC4  r1 = 0x00  r5 = 0x021DF7E8  src bytes [r5+3..5] = 00 00 00
r1 is the value about to be stored and it equals the packed composition of the three source bytes
in both cases: (0) | (0<<2) | (2<<4) = 0x20, and 0x00. So static's decode is confirmed live.

AND r5 IS THE CHARACTER HP-SLOT BASE, which locates the nature source concretely:
  r5+3, r5+4, r5+5   the three 2-bit nature slots
  r5+6               the 16-bit HP value      (0x021DF1CC+6 = 0x021DF1D2, the address I measure)
  r5+10              the ability count        (= HP+4, matching the layout already in use)
  r5+11 ...          the ability ids
So nature is stored in the per-character slot three bytes below HP, NOT in a deck-level table.
That locates static's koma lead rather than confirming it: the source is per-character, and whether
a deck writes into it is a separate question one dereference further back.

The pre-store value at [r0+0x175] read 0x3C on both sides, i.e. bits 2-5 set, before being
overwritten with 0x20 and 0x00. Unexplained; noting it rather than interpreting it.

=== 2. THE NATURE MENU DOES NOT EXIST IN EITHER BATTLE MODE I HAVE ===
This blocks the nature walk outright, and it is a documentation error rather than a harness fault.
scripts/emu/README.md documents an in-battle START menu with rows COM設定 / 自動回復 / 相手の属性,
and calls 相手の属性 "a direct lever for nature-triangle damage". I built the whole walk on it.

  fight_base (mode 0, J Arena training): a 2-frame START press opens NO menu. The DOWN and A
      presses went to the battle instead.
  dm_battle (mode 1): START opens a menu -- but it is the J ARENA PAUSE MENU, four rows:
      バトル再開 / リトライ / デッキセレクト / Jアリーナメニューにもどる
      No COM設定, no 自動回復, no 相手の属性.

So that menu belongs to DECK-MAKER TEST PLAY, a mode neither savestate is in, and the README does
not say so. Every capability I attributed to it -- setting the opponent's nature, turning auto-heal
off, making the COM fight -- is unavailable in the two battle states we actually have. That also
means my withdrawal of the deck request was wrong for the wrong reason: I withdrew it because the
menu made it unnecessary, and the menu is not reachable. The nature question needs either a
deck-maker test-play savestate or the deck build after all.

=== 3. THE BOTTOM SCREEN IS LIVE, WHICH REFUTES THE 'STATIC DECORATIVE ART' READING ===
Two independent observations on the same savestate that earlier showed plain panels:
  - after the DOWN/A presses, two koma panels acquired RED SELECTION BORDERS that were absent from
    two earlier screenshots of the same state
  - on dm_battle the pause menu RENDERS OVER the panel area
Static decorative skin art does not highlight on input and does not host a menu. So the tapped
region is live and interactive. The wrong-target explanation for the touch null (a4/8f's reading)
does not hold on this evidence, and the fourteen negatives on jus-3aw are not retired by it.

=== 4. dm_battle IS AN UNREDUCED BASELINE, WHICH NOTHING HAS MEASURED ===
Three damage-formula stops on dm_battle, all with gate word r2 = 0x00000000 and nature term r0 = 0:
  r5 = 0x300 (base byte 3), 0x500 (base 5), 0x400 (base 4)
With no gate armed and no nature term, out = r5 >> 2, so displayed damage should equal the base
byte exactly: 3.000, 5.000, 4.000. That is the zero-gate arm of the reduction question and it has
never been measured.

It also offers a better experiment than the base-2 hunt: the SAME move against fight_base's target
(gate 0x2010, class 1, so bit 4 fires) and against dm_battle's target (gate 0x0000, nothing fires)
predicts a ratio of exactly 0.750 with no dependence on finding a small base byte. Two targets, one
move, and the flat models predict a constant difference instead of a constant ratio.

=== 5. THE SELECTOR VARIES ACROSS MOVES ===
[sl+0x18] read 0x00000018 on one stop and 0x00000000 on another. Both resolve to the bits1:0 path
(0x18 & 0xC0 = 0), so this is not yet a demonstration that different moves select different nature
slots -- but it is the first evidence the field is not constant, which the wake-3 capture could not
show because every stop there returned 0x41. Static's koma lead remains untested, not refuted.

comments.author: djdjo
