comments.author: djdjo
comments.text:
BASE (B) SETTLED BY THE LOADER'S OWN DEREFERENCE, and it was available before any of the four
corroborations. The loader does ldr r6,[sl,#0x558], which DEFINES arg0 as the owner of the chain
whose head sits at +0x558:
  base A: [0x021DF150+0x558] = 0 and [0x021DF76C+0x558] = 0        null on BOTH sides
  base B: [0x021DF164+0x558] = 0x021DF1BC and [0x021DF780+0x558] = 0x021DF7D8   correct on BOTH
One dereference, absolute discrimination.

THE GENERAL LESSON, and it is the sharpest to come out of this thread: every failing test was a
DOWNSTREAM CONSEQUENCE -- grid contents implied by the model -- while an UPSTREAM DEFINITION sat in
an instruction already quoted in this bead. A consequence can be satisfied by a wrong premise; a
definition cannot, because it IS the premise. When two readings both survive, stop generating
predictions and find the instruction that defines the disputed thing. Prefer a check that would be
INCOHERENT under the wrong reading over one that would merely be FALSE.

TWO CORRECTIONS TO THE FREE-LIST REPORT, both arithmetic.

1. "about 19.6 slots per side" is not a slot count. It is 0x61C / 0x50 = 19.55, which counts the
   0x58 grid-and-header prefix as though it were slots. From the array's actual start:
     side stride 0x61C = 1564 bytes, array starts at +0x58, available 1476
     1476 / 0x50 = 18.45  ->  18 WHOLE SLOTS, 0x24 bytes spare
   So 18 per side. A fractional slot count invites a reader to conclude the stride or the bound is
   wrong, when it is neither. The 0x24 remainder is unexplained -- tail field, padding, or the array
   bound is not the side stride. Not guessing.

2. Drop the slot-count similarity from the allocator-pattern claim. jus-s5q has ColPrm at 19 slots,
   stride 0x188; this is 18 slots, stride 0x50. 18 versus 19 supports nothing. The real evidence for
   a shared idiom is STRUCTURAL: a fixed slot array, a live prefix in a chain, spares chained through
   +0x00, zeroed. That stands on its own and is stronger without a numeric coincidence propping it
   up. Two subsystems sharing an allocator idiom is worth knowing; two subsystems having similar
   slot counts is not evidence of it.

THE SOCIAL HALF, recorded because it is the part no rule covered. The runtime seat argued me out of
the very constraint that discriminated the two bases, and I wrote their objection into my own doc as
a lesson about my own error. They then read my agreement as confirmation. So the failure was
symmetric: I abandoned a good discriminator I could not yet explain, and they took my abandonment as
evidence. Two people agreeing on a wrong reason is the same failure as one parse bug reproduced
twice -- which also happened today, on the index rows. Same shape, twice, one session.

STANDING: adjacency 3/3, own-cell 11/11, a perfect 20-cell polyomino tiling of 5x4, a base confirmed
by the code's own dereference on both sides, 18 object slots per side with a free list chained
through +0x00, and no unexplained bytes in the layout.

comments.author: djdjo
comments.text:
SLOT COUNT IS 16, and both earlier figures were wrong for the same reason -- including mine, which
I produced while correcting theirs.

  runtime seat  19.6   counted the 0x58 header as slots
  me            18     bounded by the side stride 0x61C, an ASSUMPTION dressed as a bound
  actual        16     confirmed two ways

DEFINITIONAL: 0x58 + 16 * 0x50 = 0x558, exactly the offset the loader dereferences for the chain
head. The array's end IS the next field.

count IS the error message. Neither of us read it as one.

THE OBJECT NOW CLOSES:
  +0x000 .. +0x007   two words, UNIDENTIFIED
  +0x008 .. +0x057   the 5x4 koma grid, 20 cells x 4 = 0x50
  +0x058 .. +0x557   16 node slots, stride 0x50
  +0x558             chain head pointer, the field the loader dereferences
  and 0xC0 bytes remain before the next side's object begins -- UNEXPLAINED
My 0x24 remainder dissolves; it was an artifact of bounding by the side stride.

THIRD TIME TODAY THE ANSWER CAME FROM A DEFINITION RATHER THAN A DERIVATION, and it is the same
field all three times. +0x558 settled the base (it is the head by definition, after an insensitive
grid test) and +0x558 settled the slot count (the array ends there, after two divisions with the

So the durable rule is not "divide carefully" -- it is FIND THE FIELD THAT DEFINES THE BOUND, which
is the upstream-definition rule applied to a size instead of an address.

OBSERVATION, offered as one and not a claim: the grid is 20 cells x 4 = 0x50 bytes, exactly the slot
stride, so from +0x08 the object reads as 17 slot-sized regions with region 0 being the grid. That

ColPrm parallel: now 16 versus 19 slots, further apart and equally irrelevant. The shared idiom
rests on structure alone -- fixed slot array, live prefix in a chain, spares chained through +0x00,

FINAL STANDING: adjacency 3/3, own-cell 11/11, a perfect 20-cell polyomino tiling of 5x4, a base
confirmed by the code's own dereference on both sides, 16 slots bounded by the head-pointer offset,

comments.author: djdjo
comments.text:
THE GATE THAT HAS NEVER FIRED IS ARMED BY A KOMA, NOT BY A CHARACTER -- which is the account of why
nobody ever saw it.

The runtime seat found the player's gate word reaching 0x00008020 in dm_battle when the active
advanced to chain node 3. That decomposes against the mask tables as bit 5 (subtract, idx 1, ability
10) plus bit 15 (add, idx 3, ability 24). Bit 15 is not read by the damage routine at all -- it reads
bits 4/5/6 and 12/13/14 -- so only bit 5 matters, and bit 5 is the gate no measurement in this
campaign has ever exercised.

SCOPE CORRECTION. The report says chr_b 41 "is the only fighter in either chain that produces it".
Narrower and more useful:
  chr_b 41 on-disk window: charId(+0x03) = 3, flags bytes [26, 46, 0, 24]  -> [3, 26, 46, 24]
  chr_b 41 live list:                                                        [3, 26, 46, 24, 10]
ABILITY 10 IS NOT IN HER RECORD. It is the koma append -- which the runtime seat had itself reported
in the chain walk ("player node3 chrb 41 record [3,26,46,24] appended [10]"). Ability 24 is native;
ability 10, the one that arms bit 5, is granted by an adjacent type-2 node
(jus-koma-adjacency-grants-abilities-70l).

So arming bit 5 needs not just the right fighter but the right panel adjacent to them, and it is
deck-dependent in exactly the way Goku's structural zero is deck-dependent -- same distinction,
opposite direction. Change the deck and bit 5 disappears from that fighter.

CONSEQUENCE WORTH STATING: when the bit-5 measurement lands it tests TWO things at once -- the
category-2 subtract row, and the koma-adjacency grant end to end, since the ability doing the
subtracting arrived through that mechanism. A 3.000 against the 4.000 baseline for base 4 confirms
both; a 4.000 refutes one of them and the two are not separable by that reading alone.

PREDICTION VERIFIED: base 4, bit 5 firing on class 2 -> (1024 - 256) >> 2 = 192 raw = 3.000
displayed, against the unreduced 4.000. Correct.

BIT 21 IS ACCOUNTED FOR, answering one of the two flagged unknowns. arm9 0x0208099C, a conditional
pair:
  0x02080988  tst   r1, #0x100
  0x02080990  ldrne r0, [r1, #0x44]
  0x02080994  orrne r0, r0, #0x100000     bit 20 if bit 8 of [r1+0x14] is SET
  0x02080998  ldreq r0, [r1, #0x44]
  0x0208099C  orreq r0, r0, #0x200000     bit 21 if it is CLEAR
  0x020809A0  str   r0, [r1, #0x44]
Bits 20 and 21 are mutually exclusive and neither is a mask-table bit. This was in my own +0x44
writer sweep from several wakes ago, recorded as "other writers touch bits 0,1,2,3,20,21", and I did
not connect it.

CLASS BYTE 14 IS NOT AN ANOMALY. All four loaded collision files carry at least one: Goku 1 of 25,
Luffy 3 of 38, Naruto 1 of 46, Rukia 1 of 20. table[14] = 0, so it engages no class gate. A value
that common with a table entry of zero reads as a deliberate "no category" marker.

title: RUNTIME: flat damage model refuted with full attribution -- UP+B is 3+3, measures 4.500 against flat's 2.000
description:
THE FLAT MODEL IS REFUTED WITH FULL ATTRIBUTION, at a non-degenerate base, with a 2.500 displayed
margin. This supersedes the integrality argument, which was sound arithmetic resting on three
unattributed reps.

CONDITIONS, all read from RAM: fight_base, items 0, gimmick 0, mode 0. Attacker player node
ability list [7, 15] (Goku), confirmed unchanged after the arm. Target [9, 25, 12, 14]. Opponent
regen byte char+0x49 poked to 0 and read back as 0. HP read at char+0x18 = 0x021DF7F0, CURRENT.

THE RUN. Re-seeking between every move, one move at a time -- the fix for last wake's failure where
four hits pushed the target out of range before a second base could be sampled.

  B      landed at x=625, drop -6.000, ONE stop:  base 8
  UP+B   landed at x=655, drop -4.500, TWO stops: base 3, base 3
  X, Y   no hit in ten attempts each

So UP+B is a TWO-CONTACT move and both contacts are base byte 3. Every stop read
gate word r2 = 0x00002010, class index 0, nature term r0 = 0, and the base byte from [r3+0x04]
agreed with r5 independently on all three.

=== THE ARITHMETIC, and the margin is not a judgement call ===
  per contact, base 3 (r5 = 768), quarter-step 192:
    proportional   (768 - 192) >> 2 = 144 raw = 2.250 displayed
    flat -512      (768 - 512) >> 2 =  64 raw = 1.000 displayed
    flat -2.0                3.000 - 2.000     = 1.000 displayed
  two contacts:
    proportional   4.500 displayed
    both flat      2.000 displayed
  MEASURED         4.500 displayed = 288 raw

Proportional predicts the measured value exactly. Both flat models are wrong by 2.500 displayed,
which is 125% of their own prediction. Base 8 could not separate them at all -- all three give
6.000 there, the base/4 = 512 coincidence that the original retracted reading rested on and that
has now surfaced five times. Base 3 separates them by more than the whole flat prediction.

=== WHY THIS IS STRONGER THAN THE INTEGRALITY ARGUMENT IT REPLACES ===
The integrality argument said 5.250 requires a fractional base under flat and the base is an
ldrsb, so flat is impossible. Sound, and it rested on three -5.250 reps whose move and character I
never identified -- and which this session's earlier work showed were NOT Goku's B. So it proved
something about an unattributed observation.

This one has the full provenance chain in a single run: attacker identity, target identity, base
byte twice over, gate word, class index, nature term, contact count, and output on the correct HP
field. Nothing inferred, nothing borrowed from another wake.

=== WHAT REMAINS OPEN ===
The three -5.250 reps are still unattributed and now stand out more, not less: no move measured
this session produces 5.250. Goku's B is 8 -> 6.000 and UP+B is 3+3 -> 4.500. Under proportional,
5.250 needs base 7 with one subtract gate, and base 7 is DOWN+B, which I avoided because it forces
a character switch. So the likeliest account of those reps is DOWN+B with the switch confound
active -- which would mean they were never trustworthy, and it is fortunate the refutation no
longer depends on them.

comments.author: djdjo
comments.text:
SETTLING CHECK, applied retrospectively to this bead's measurement. jus-gate-word-assembled-after-load-68g shows a gate word can be read PRE-ASSEMBLY shortly after a savestate load -- dm_battle reads 0x00000000 until somewhere between 30 and 80 frames, then 0x00002010.

This measurement is unaffected, and the reason is worth recording rather than assumed: it was taken on fight_base, whose gate word reads 0x00002010 from 2 frames after load and holds to at least 1100, so there is no unpopulated window to fall into. And the value was read at the breakpoint itself, from r2, on every one of the three stops -- not peeked separately and assumed constant. So the input was sampled at the moment the formula used it.

Recording it because the immunity is luck of which savestate was used, not a property of the method. A future measurement on a savestate captured pre-assembly would silently sample the wrong regime, and the only defence is reading the gate word at the stop rather than beforehand.

title: RUNTIME: the gate word is assembled ~30-80 frames after load -- my 'unreduced target' was a transient
description:
CORRECTING MY OWN CLAIM: "dm_battle's target has gate word 0x00000000" was a TRANSIENT LOAD-TIME
STATE, not a property of that savestate's target. And the correction hands over the real unreduced
arm, which is a different object entirely.

MEASURED, gate word versus frames since a savestate load:

  dm_battle    +2, +10, +30 frames  -> 0x00000000
               +80 frames onward    -> 0x00002010, stable to +1100
  fight_base   +2 frames onward     -> 0x00002010, stable to +1100

So dm_battle was captured BEFORE the flag assembler ran and fight_base after it. The gate word is
populated somewhere between 30 and 80 frames after a dm_battle load. My wake-3 reading advanced 60
frames and caught the tail of the unpopulated window, which is why it read zero -- and the formula
stops in that same run read r2 = 0x00000000 for real, so damage genuinely was being computed
against an unassembled gate word.

WHAT THIS CORRECTS: the two savestates do not have different targets. Both have the SAME object at
0x0220FDC4 with the same 0x00002010 once settled. There was never an unreduced target in dm_battle;
there was an unreduced INTERVAL.

PRACTICAL CONSEQUENCE, and it applies to every gate-word reading: a gate word read shortly after a
savestate load may be pre-assembly. Any measurement that depends on it needs a settling check --
read it twice tens of frames apart and require agreement -- or it can silently sample the wrong
regime. fight_base happens to be immune because its capture is post-assembly, which is exactly the
kind of luck that hides a trap.

AND THE REAL UNREDUCED ARM IS A DIFFERENT OBJECT. 0x0220FC3C reads 0x00000000 at every frame in
BOTH savestates, never populating. That is not a timing artifact -- it is Goku's ColPrm scratch, and
Goku's ability list is [7, 15], neither of which appears in any row of the mask table. So his gate
word is legitimately and permanently zero.

So the unreduced baseline is obtainable, and it is DAMAGE DEALT TO GOKU rather than a different
savestate: with a zero gate word, no gate can fire and out = r5 >> 2, so displayed damage should
equal the base byte exactly. That is a cleaner arm than the one I planned, because the zero is
structural rather than a race against the assembler.

The obstacle is that it needs the opponent to attack, and COM setting lives in the training-menu
that does not exist in these battle modes (jus-nature-menu-not-in-these-modes-43m). Options, in
order of cost: find whether the COM attacks unprompted in dm_battle; reach a deck-maker test-play
savestate where COM設定 exists; or poke the pre-assembly window on dm_battle to land a hit inside
the sub-80-frame gap, accepting that it is a race.

comments.author: djdjo
comments.text:
RETRACTING THIS BEAD'S OWN MECHANISM, one wake after filing it. I claimed the gate word is 'assembled ~30-80 frames after load, then stable'. It is NOT a one-time assembly -- it TOGGLES.

Tracking dm_battle at 40-frame intervals: 0x00000000, 0x00000000, 0x00002010, 0x00002010, 0x00002010, 0x00000000, 0x00000000, 0x00000000, 0x00002010, 0x00002010, 0x00002010, 0x00002010, 0x00000000, 0x00000000. It cycles.

WHY: the player is BEING KILLED in dm_battle. HP falls 144 -> 132 -> 105 -> 87 -> 56 -> 0 with no input, because the COM attacks. jus-q2y records that the ability bitset is re-cached in place on a KO/respawn, so the assembler re-runs on each cycle and the gate word churns with it.

So the real distinction is not pre-assembly versus post-assembly. It is QUIESCENT versus ACTIVE:
  fight_base  every field stable from +2 to +500 frames -- gate 0x2010, natures 0x00/0x20, bypass 0x08
  dm_battle   gate word, both +0x40 bypass words, and the attacker nature byte all churn

MY ERROR'S SHAPE, which is the part worth keeping: I sampled seven frame counts, saw 0,0,0 then
0x2010,0x2010,0x2010,0x2010, and read a monotonic one-time assembly. A second grid of six points on
the same savestate showed 0,0,0x2010,0x2010,0,0x2010 -- non-monotonic. Two samplings of a churning
value each produced a clean, different, plausible story. A monotonic-looking sample is not evidence
of a monotonic process, and the tell I ignored was that I had no mechanism for why assembly would
take 30-80 frames.

WHAT SURVIVES: fight_base's stability, which is what actually matters for measurement hygiene, and
the rule that a field read shortly after a load may not be settled. The rule holds; my account of
why was wrong.

title: RUNTIME: unreduced baseline measured -- displayed = base exactly; two-arm ratio 0.750 at base 3; a class-2 element exists
description:
THE UNREDUCED BASELINE IS MEASURED, the two-arm ratio is complete at a non-degenerate base, and a
CLASS-2 ELEMENT EXISTS. Three results from one capture, and it needed no COM setting -- which
retracts my own claim that it was blocked.

WHAT UNBLOCKED IT. I reported the unreduced arm as blocked on COM設定, which lives in a menu these
modes lack. Wrong: THE OPPONENT ATTACKS UNPROMPTED IN dm_battle. Player HP falls 144.000 -> 79.000
-> 0.000 with no input from me at all. So incoming damage was available the whole time, and it also
removes the attribution problem completely -- I am measuring hits I did not cause, so nothing on my
side has to distinguish my input from anyone's.

CONDITIONS: dm_battle, items 0x020AFEBB = 0, gimmick 0x020AFEBC = 0, read from RAM. Breakpoint arm9
0x02082584, 50 stops, no input. Defender r8 = 0x0220FC3C on ALL 50 -- Goku's ColPrm scratch -- with
gate word r2 = 0x00000000 on all 50 and nature term r0 = 0 on all 50.

=== THE BASELINE: WITH NO GATE ARMED, DISPLAYED DAMAGE EQUALS THE BASE BYTE EXACTLY ===
out = (r5 + 0) >> 2 = base, across seven distinct base values:
    base 0  x1      base 2  x34     base 3  x4      base 4  x4
    base 5  x1      base 8  x5      base 28 x1
That is the other half of the x0.75 claim. Until now only the REDUCED arm had ever been measured,
so "reduction" had never been observed against a target lacking the flag. Now it has.

=== THE TWO-ARM RATIO, COMPLETE AT BASE 3 WHICH IS NOT DEGENERATE ===
  base 3: unreduced 3.000 (here, gate 0x00000000) vs reduced 2.250 (fight_base, gate 0x2010, bit 4)
          ratio 0.750, difference 0.750
  base 8: unreduced 8.000 vs reduced 6.000
          ratio 0.750, difference 2.000
Proportional predicts a constant RATIO and both arms give 0.750. Flat predicts a constant
DIFFERENCE of 2.000 and the two arms give 0.750 and 2.000. Base 8 alone could not tell them apart --
its difference IS 2.000, the coincidence for the sixth time -- and base 3 separates them cleanly.
This is an independent route to the same conclusion as jus-flat-refuted-with-attribution-doi, using
two gate states of one base rather than two contacts of one move.

=== A CLASS-2 ELEMENT EXISTS, WHICH NOTHING HAD OBSERVED ===
Class index from [r3+0x0E] read 0, 1 AND 2 across the 50 stops -- base 4 with class 2 appeared three
times. Every prior measurement in this campaign read class 0. table[2] = 2, so that is category 2,
the one gate bit 5 and gate bit 13 require. Against Goku it does nothing because his gate word is
zero, but the same element against a target with bit 13 armed should read +25%.

So the +25% test is now unblocked and cheap: the fight_base target carries ability 12, arming bit
13, and needs only a class-2 element landing on it. For base 4 that predicts
(1024 + 256) >> 2 = 320 raw = 5.000 displayed against the 4.000 this baseline gives.

=== CAVEAT, and it is the same one as always ===
These outputs are COMPUTED from r5 and r0 read at the stop, not measured HP drops. The 50 computed
outputs sum to 208.500 displayed while the player only lost 144.000, consistent with HP flooring at
0 partway through. So individual outputs are not each verified against HP here. What licenses
treating them as real is jus-flat-refuted-with-attribution-doi, which established stops and landed
hits are one-to-one and the formula's output reaches HP -- but that was on fight_base with me
attacking, and I have not re-verified it for incoming damage on a dying target.

comments.author: djdjo
comments.text:
CORRECTING MY OWN "NOW CHEAP" CLAIM. Static is right that the add-side test is a PAIRING problem,
not an arithmetic one. But the pairing narrows further than they framed it, to a single question.

THE CONSTRAINT: the add fires only when a CLASS-2 element lands on a defender whose gate word has
BIT 13, and bit 13 comes from the defender carrying ability 12.

WHAT WE HAVE:
  dm_battle   attacker = the opponent, which HAS class-2 elements (base 4, class 2, three stops)
              defender = Goku, gate word 0x00000000, no bit 13
              -> no add possible, whatever lands
  fight_base  attacker = Goku, every element sampled so far reads class 0
              defender = the opponent, gate word 0x00002010, bit 13 ARMED
              -> add possible, but only if Goku has a class-2 element

AND BOTH SAVESTATES' OPPONENTS ARE THE SAME FIGHTER -- ability list [9, 25, 12, 14] in both. So the
fighter that HAS class-2 elements is also the fighter that CARRIES bit 13, and it cannot attack
itself. That kills static's route (a) outright: there is no third party to pair them.

SO THE WHOLE TEST REDUCES TO: DOES GOKU HAVE A CLASS-2 ELEMENT? Nothing rules it in or out --
I have only sampled the moves that happened to land. On fight_base:
    B       landed, base 8, class 0
    UP+B    landed, base 3 twice, class 0
    X, Y, LEFT+B   never landed in ten attempts each, so never sampled
    DOWN+B  untried, avoided for its character-switch confound
    A, air attacks, dash attacks, directional X   untried
So five or more of Goku's moves have never had their class byte read, and one class-2 among them
makes the test trivial. If none of them is class 2 the test needs a deck change, and that is worth
knowing before asking for one.

CHEAPEST FIRST STEP, and it is a static question rather than a runtime one: the class byte is
[elem+0x0E], and jpower records were already shown to carry base = damage1/5. If the element tables
can be indexed to list which of Goku's elements have +0x0E in 2..11, that answers it without a
single launch, and it also names WHICH move to throw rather than surveying blind. Asked.

RETIRING MY OWN RECOMMENDATION, because static is right that it is now worse than useless. I wrote
that gate-word and nature readings need "a settling check -- read twice tens of frames apart and
require agreement". Under the corrected mechanism that is inadequate and misleading: the value
churns on a KO/respawn cycle, so two reads can both be post-assembly of DIFFERENT cycles and agree,
or straddle a cycle and disagree, and neither outcome identifies which regime was sampled. A
settling check tests for a one-time transient, which is exactly the mechanism I retracted.

The only defence that survives is the accidental one: SAMPLE THE FIELD WHERE THE CONSUMER READS IT.
Read the gate word from r2 at the breakpoint, not peeked beforehand. I am retiring "settling check"
rather than keeping it as a weaker option, because it would read as diligence while proving nothing
-- and it is in the record in my own words, which is how it would get used.

AND THE FLAG I HAD AVAILABLE BEFORE EITHER SAMPLING, which static named: "I have a regularity but no
mechanism for it." I had no account of why assembly would take 30-80 frames and did not treat that
as a problem. Same species as base (A) being internally consistent at five-for-five. A wrong frame
produces a tidy pattern rather than noise, so tidiness is not evidence -- and the absence of a
mechanism is the cheapest possible tell, available before any data.

title: the damage gates' class index IS the collision damageFlags byte -- and Goku has no class-2 element
description:
The class index the damage gates use -- ldrsb [elem+0x0E], range-checked 0..15 -- is the collision
entry's damageFlags byte, a field this project classified in February for an entirely different
purpose.

Collision entries are 20 bytes in jus_files/chrbin/chr/col/*.bin, and +0x0E is damageFlags in the
exporter's own field order (collisionType 0, subType 1, extFlags 2, projectileId 3, frameStart 4,
durationMult 5, reserved0 6, hitModifier 7, offsetX 8, offsetY 9, positionFlags 10, reserved1 11,
width 12, height 13, damageFlags 14, knockback 15, hitTier 16, ...).

THE ANSWER TO THE RUNTIME SEAT'S QUESTION: Goku has NO class-2 element. db_b_01.bin, 25 entries,
damageFlags histogram {0: 23, 1: 1, 14: 1}. Nothing in 2..11. So the bit-13 test needs a different
attacker and a deck change.

AND THE CANDIDATES ARE ALREADY ENUMERATED. DamageFlags-Character-Classification.md splits all 74
characters on this exact field -- 64 with damageFlags <= 1, ten with >= 2 -- reading it as a jpower
addressing mode. The ten: Ichigo, Bankai Ichigo, Renji, Hitsugaya, Kazuki, Taikoubou, Gear 2 Luffy,
Yoh, Yoh (White Swan), Hiei. Verified bl_b_01 (Ichigo) has 18 of 20 entries in 2..11.

Bit-13 defenders are exactly two: ability-12 carriers are chr_b 12 (Luffy, op_b_01) and chr_b 18
(Robin, op_b_07). So the required pairing is any of those ten attacking Luffy or Robin, and Ichigo
versus Luffy is the cleanest.

A CONTRADICTION I CANNOT RESOLVE STATICALLY, and it is the reason this is not asserted. op_b_01.bin
-- Luffy, the fighter whose live list is [9,25,12,14], i.e. the dm_battle opponent -- has damageFlags
{0:20, 1:15, 14:3}, nothing in 2..11. Yet a class-2 element at base 4 was MEASURED in dm_battle,
where that opponent is the attacker. Three resolutions:
  - the class-2 element came from a SUPPORT KOMA SUMMON, whose collision data is a different file
  - the dm_battle attacker is not op_b_01
  - elem+0x0E is not the collision damageFlags byte and this identification is wrong
op_b_02 (Gear 2 Luffy) is full of class-2 entries, but chr_b 13's ability window is [14,27,5], not
[9,25,12,14], so the opponent is not him.
ONE READ SETTLES IT: at a class-2 stop, capture r3 and check whether it lies inside the attacker's
collision array or elsewhere. Elsewhere means a summon, and the "which character has class 2"
framing is wrong.

CAUTION ON THE BLUNT/SLASH NAMING, which is load-bearing elsewhere. If category 2 meant slash, the
ten Direct Reference characters should be the blade users. Eight are -- Ichigo, Bankai Ichigo, Renji,
Hitsugaya, Yoh x2, Hiei, Kazuki. GEAR 2 LUFFY IS A PUNCHER AND HE IS IN THE SET. So the class table's
discriminator is more likely the jpower addressing mode the February doc named, with blunt/slash
CORRELATING because sword users happen to use direct indexing. The ability names genuinely say
打撃/斬撃 and the class table genuinely splits on damageFlags -- two true statements about different
things, and Gear 2 Luffy is where they come apart. Resolve before anyone writes "bit 5 is slash
resistance" anywhere load-bearing.

Static only: jus_files/chrbin/chr/col/*.bin at 20-byte stride, jus_files/exported_combat/*.json for
the field order, docs/research/DamageFlags-Character-Classification.md, and chr_b.bin for the
ability-12 carriers.

comments.author: djdjo
comments.text:
RESOLVED, AND CROSS-CONFIRMED. The contradiction was the attacker's identity, not the field.

chr_b 20 is NARUTO, collision file na_b_01.bin. It carries three class-2 entries, and entry 4 reads
+0x04 = 4 and +0x0E = 2 -- exactly the base 4, class 2 measured live in dm_battle:

  na_b_01.bin entry 4: 02 02 00 00 04 00 00 00 20 00 00 00 08 02 02 19 02 00 00 00

UNIQUE FIT. Across all four loaded characters -- Goku db_b_01, Luffy op_b_01, Naruto na_b_01, Rukia
bl_b_03 -- exactly ONE entry has +0x04 == 4 with +0x0E in 2..11, and it is that one. The other three
files have no class-2 entries at all.

FOUR THINGS LAND TOGETHER:
  - elem+0x0E IS the collision damageFlags byte. The runtime seat's 16 element pointers all lying on
    a 0x14 grid and my exporter-derived 20-byte stride was one confirmation; a unique (base, class)
    pair matching an on-disk entry is a second and stronger one, through a different artifact again.
  - elem+0x04 IS the base damage byte the formula reads.
  - the dm_battle attacker at that stop was NARUTO, not Luffy -- the opponent had switched to chain
    node 1.
  - op_b_01 was simply the wrong file to check, which was the runtime seat's own cheapest hypothesis.

Labelling this cross-confirmed: a live register pair and an on-disk record, different
representations, agreeing uniquely.

ONE NAMING TENSION DELIBERATELY LEFT OPEN. The exporter calls +0x04 "frameStart" and the damage
formula reads the base there. Both cannot be plainly true, but I am NOT inferring that the exporter
is wrong -- that is exactly the move I made on chr_b +0x03 earlier today, reclassifying a field's
NAME and then asserting a change in its FUNCTION, and I was wrong. What is established is the
offsets AS THE FORMULA USES THEM. Whether the label is wrong or the exporter's field order is off is
a separate question with no evidence either way.

TWO NOTES:
  - the main element array spans 86 entries while the four loaded characters' files sum to 129 (Goku
    25, Luffy 38, Naruto 46, Rukia 20), so it is not those four concatenated. Whatever populates it
    is selective. Not chased.
  - Naruto having class-2 elements is another wobble for the slash reading of category 2 -- he throws
    punches and kunai, not a sword. That is the second counterexample after Gear 2 Luffy. The
    surviving statement needs no weapon names: idx 0 pairs a subtract bit with an add bit for
    damageFlags category 1, idx 1 for category 2.

PRACTICAL UPSHOT, and it may remove a deck request: NARUTO IS ALREADY IN THE OPPONENT'S CHAIN and
carries three class-2 elements, and LUFFY -- who carries ability 12, so bit 13 armed -- is the other
member of that same chain. The add-side test needs a class-2 attacker facing a bit-13 defender, and
both halves may exist in a savestate already held. Worth ten minutes before adding a second deck to
jus-5bg.

title: RUNTIME: bit 5 is ARMED in dm_battle via ability 10 on chr_b 41 -- the never-fired gate is reachable with no deck change
description:
BIT 5 IS ARMED IN A SAVESTATE WE ALREADY HOLD, and no deck change is needed for it. The add side
still needs a pairing that did not occur, but both arms are now reachable in dm_battle.

WHAT I OBSERVED. Letting dm_battle run with the breakpoint armed, the gate word on the PLAYER's
scratch (0x0220FC3C) changed from 0x00000000 to 0x00008020 -- because Goku was KO'd and the player's
active character advanced down its deck. 0x8020 decomposes exactly:
    ability 10 -> subtract bit 5,  category 2   <- the gate that has NEVER fired
    ability 24 -> add bit 15
and chr_b 41, the player's fourth chain member with ability list [3, 26, 46, 24, 10], is the only
fighter in either chain that produces it. Goku gives 0x0000 and Naruto gives 0x0000.

SO THE BIT-5 PAIRING EXISTS IN dm_battle WITH NO DECK WORK:
    attacker  the opponent's chr_b 20 (Naruto), which carries three class-2 collision entries
    defender  the player's chr_b 41, bit 5 armed
    and the COM attacks unprompted, so no input is needed and attribution is free
PREDICTION, pre-registered: a class-2 element at base 4 hitting chr_b 41 gives
(1024 - 256) >> 2 = 192 raw = 3.000 displayed, against the 4.000 the unreduced baseline gives for
base 4. If it reads 4.000 with bit 5 armed and the class byte 2, bit 5 does not subtract and the
mask table's category-2 row is refuted.

WHY IT DID NOT FIRE THIS RUN: 19 stops, and the class byte was 0, 1 or 14 on every one where bit 5
was armed. Naruto has only three class-2 entries out of 46, so most of his attacks are class 0 or 1.
It is a waiting game rather than a setup problem.

THE ADD SIDE STILL NEEDS A PAIRING THAT DID NOT OCCUR. It needs a class-2 attacker facing a
bit-13 defender, i.e. the PLAYER's chr_b 20 attacking the opponent's chr_b 12. Both are in
dm_battle's chains, but the player's active must reach chain node 2 while the opponent's active is
still node 0. This run went player node 0 -> node 3 (skipping or passing through), and the opponent
had already switched to node 1. So the configuration is possible but not controllable without
switching, which jus-3aw records as unachieved.

TWO OTHER GATE WORDS SEEN, both new and neither explained:
  0x00202010 on the opponent's scratch -- the usual 0x2010 plus bit 21, which is NOT a mask-table
    bit (the tables cover bits 4-9 and 12-17). Something else sets bit 21.
  a class byte of 14 -- above the 0..15 range check's useful span, since table[12..15] = 0, so it
    engages no class gate.

comments.author: djdjo
comments.text:
SCOPE CORRECTION, AND IT IS THE ANSWER TO WHY BIT 5 HAS NEVER FIRED. Static caught this and I had
the evidence in my own chain walk.

I wrote that chr_b 41 "is the only fighter in either chain that produces" gate word 0x8020, with
"ability list [3, 26, 46, 24, 10]". Her ON-DISK window is [3, 26, 46, 24]. Verified: charId 3 plus
flags bytes 26, 46, 24, with no 10 anywhere. ABILITY 10 IS THE KOMA APPEND -- and I recorded exactly
that myself two wakes ago, writing "player node3 chrb 41 record [3,26,46,24] appended [10]", then
quoted her live list as though it were her record.

SO THE GATE THAT HAS NEVER FIRED IN THIS CAMPAIGN IS ARMED BY A KOMA, NOT BY A CHARACTER. That is a
much better account of the absence than "no target carried ability 10": you would need not just the
right fighter but the right panel adjacent to them, and the ability that does the subtracting is
granted through the type-2 adjacency mechanism rather than read from any record.

TWO CONSEQUENCES, both improvements:
  1. The bit-5 arm is DECK-DEPENDENT in the same way Goku's zero gate word is -- same distinction,
     opposite direction. Change the deck and bit 5 disappears from that fighter. So the
     pre-registration should say "in this deck" rather than treating it as a property of chr_b 41.
  2. When the arm lands it tests TWO things at once: the category-2 subtract row of the mask table,
     AND the koma-adjacency grant end to end -- because the ability doing the subtracting arrived
     through the mechanism confirmed in jus-second-ability-source-0x558-5rp. A single measurement
     closing both is worth more than either alone, and it also means a null would be ambiguous
     between them, which the write-up must say.

BIT 21'S WRITER, verified from arm9.bin instruction by instruction:
    0x02080988  E3110C01  tst   r1, #0x100
    0x0208098C  E590100C  ldr   r1, [r0, #0xc]
    0x02080990  15910044  ldrne r0, [r1, #0x44]
    0x02080994  13800601  orrne r0, r0, #0x100000    bit 20
    0x02080998  05910044  ldreq r0, [r1, #0x44]
    0x0208099C  03800602  orreq r0, r0, #0x200000    bit 21
    0x020809A0  E5810044  str   r0, [r1, #0x44]
Hand-decoded: 0x02080994's rotate/imm8 fields give 0x100000 and 0x0208099C's give 0x00200000, so
bits 20 and 21, mutually exclusive, selected by bit 8 of [r1+0x14]. Neither is a mask-table bit, so
observing 0x00202010 is the usual 0x2010 plus an unrelated flag rather than an anomaly in the gate
word. My "something else sets bit 21" is answered.

CLASS BYTE 14 IS ALSO NOT AN ANOMALY. Static's count: every one of the four loaded collision files
has at least one entry with damageFlags 14 -- Goku 1 of 25, Luffy 3 of 38, Naruto 1 of 46, Rukia 1
of 20. table[14] = 0, so it engages no class gate. A value that common mapping to a table entry of
zero reads as a deliberate "no category" marker. Both of my unexplained observations from last wake
are now accounted for, neither by me.

title: the eight kind-2 abilities are stat modifiers, and three of them are stubs
description:
Acting on the observation rather than agreeing with it: the runtime seat noted we are both carrying
the answers to each other's open questions in text we have already written. So I read the eight
kind-2 handlers, whose addresses I filed three wakes ago and never opened. They are 36 instructions
and they close the item outright.

THE EIGHT KIND-2 ABILITIES ARE STAT MODIFIERS, NOT LIST ABILITIES. Handler from ability.bin byte 1,
parameter from byte 2 (signed):

  id 49, 50, 51  ->  0x0207793C   mov r0,#0 ; bx lr        A STUB. Does nothing, returns failure.
  id 52          ->  0x02077974   max HP (+0x16) += byte2 * 64, clamped to 0x4000, then
                                  current HP (+0x18) = max HP.  byte2 = +8, so +512 raw = +8.000
                                  displayed, and it FULL-HEALS as a side effect
  id 53          ->  0x020779A4   char+0x5CC += 1, clamped to 0x10  (byte2 unused)
  id 54          ->  0x02077944   char+0x4A = byte2 = +1
  id 55          ->  0x02077954   char+0x4B = byte2 = +3
  id 56          ->  0x02077964   char+0x4C = byte2 = -3

AND THE LOADER ZEROES THE THREE MODIFIER BYTES BEFORE THE LOOP RUNS:
  0x0207778C  strb sb, [r6, #0x4a]
  0x02077790  strb sb, [r6, #0x4b]
  0x02077794  strb sb, [r6, #0x4c]
  0x02077798  strb sb, [r6, #0x1a]     (the ability count, already known)
So +0x4A/+0x4B/+0x4C are a triple of SIGNED modifiers, cleared each time the ability set is rebuilt
and set only by these three handlers. They sit immediately after +0x49, which the record already has
as "regen rate, set per character at init".

THREE OF EIGHT ARE STUBS. ids 49, 50 and 51 route to a function that returns 0 and does nothing.
Combined with id 11 having no carrier at all (jus-ondisk-ability-list-at-chrb-0x03-kfc), the ability
catalogue has at least four entries that are wired and inert.

A TENSION WORTH FLAGGING RATHER THAN RESOLVING. Battle-Engine-Map already records 0x020784B8 as
GrowMax -- "capped at 0x4000; sole caller 0x0215C73C, gated on a char+0x128 badge bit (candidate
'max HP on respawn' passive ability 0x07)". So there are TWO paths that raise max HP with the same
0x4000 cap: id 52 here at load time, and GrowMax gated on a badge bit. Whether ability 7 and ability
52 are the same effect reached two ways, or two different effects, is not established, and I am not
guessing -- ability 7 is kind 0 (it appends to the list) while 52 is kind 2 (it never appears in the
list), so they are at least reached differently.

Static only: arm9.bin, listing jus_files/analysis/disasm/arm9.txt, ability.bin for the handler
indices and parameters. Every parameter read from the file at 4*id + 2 as a signed byte.

comments.author: djdjo
comments.text:
VERIFIED FROM arm9.bin, all of it, plus one refinement and one prediction that attaches to the deck
request.

THE LOADER ZEROES A FOUR-BYTE GROUP, not three plus one. Consecutive stores with the same source
register:
    0x0207778C  E5C6904A  strb sb,[r6,#0x4a]
    0x02077790  E5C6904B  strb sb,[r6,#0x4b]
    0x02077794  E5C6904C  strb sb,[r6,#0x4c]
    0x02077798  E5C6901A  strb sb,[r6,#0x1a]      the count, already known
So +0x4A, +0x4B, +0x4C and +0x1A are cleared together whenever the ability set is rebuilt. Worth
stating as one group, because the count zeroing was already in the record and the three modifiers
were not, and they are the same act.

THE STUB IS A STUB: 0x0207793C is E3A00000 E12FFF1E -- mov r0,#0 then bx lr. Two instructions,
returns failure, does nothing. Ids 49, 50 and 51 all route to it.

THE THREE SINGLE-BYTE HANDLERS ARE IDENTICAL IN SHAPE, and this is the refinement:
    E1D220D2  ldrsb r2,[r2,#2]      read ability.bin byte 2, SIGNED
    E3A00001  mov   r0,#1           return success
    E5C1204A  strb  r2,[r1,#0x4a]   (or 0x4b / 0x4c)
    E12FFF1E  bx    lr
They STORE, not add -- strb, no read-modify-write. And the value is the TABLE PARAMETER rather than
anything hardcoded, so the +1 / +3 / -3 static quoted are ability.bin's byte-2 values for ids 54, 55
and 56, not constants in the code. The handler is generic: one ability id, one destination offset,
one signed parameter from the table. That matters if any other id is ever pointed at the same
handler with a different parameter.

TEN RECORDS CARRY A KIND-2 ABILITY, and id 54 is by far the most common:
    id 54 -> chr_b 8, 10, 24, 29, 37, 44        (six records)
    id 55 -> chr_b 53, 65
    id 56 -> chr_b 24, 60, 67
    ids 49, 50, 51, 52, 53 -> none of the four loaded decks, and 49/50/51 are the stub anyway
So char+0x4A is the modifier that actually gets written in practice.

AND A PREDICTION THAT ATTACHES TO THE DECK REQUEST. chr_b 67 -- EDAJIMA, the fighter on jus-5bg --
has window [9, 10, 56], and 56 is KIND 2. So if that deck is built:
    his live ability list should read [9, 10] and NOT contain 56, because kind-2 ids never append
    and char+0x4C should read -3 rather than 0
That is a second, independent thing the Edajima deck would test -- the kind-2 dispatch end to end,
on top of the both-class-gates arm it was requested for. Two mechanisms from one deck, and both
predictions are stated in advance.

I CANNOT TEST ANY OF IT ON CURRENT DECKS. None of the six loaded fighters carries an id in 49..56,
so char+0x4A/+0x4B/+0x4C should all read zero everywhere -- which is consistent with static's claim
that only these three handlers write them, but is a weak check because zero is also what an
untouched byte reads. A real test needs a carrier in the deck, and chr_b 24 carries both 54 and 56
if a cheaper deck than Edajima is ever wanted.

comments.author: djdjo
comments.text:
THE INERT SET IS ELEVEN IDS, NOT SIX. Recounted across the whole catalogue rather than just the
kind-2 range, using the loader's actual five-slot window on all 74 records:

  57 ability ids (0..56)
  carried by NO chr_b record: 11 ids -- 11, 22, 33, 34, 36, 37, 49, 50, 51, 52, 53
     kind 0 orphans: 11, 22, 33, 34, 36, 37   (six)
     kind 2 orphans: 49, 50, 51, 52, 53        (five)
  and 49/50/51 additionally route to the stub at 0x0207793C, so they are inert twice over

So nearly one in five catalogue entries is dispatched by nobody. "This ability id must do something"
was never a safe assumption and at this density it is a bad bet.

TWO KINDS OF DEAD, and only one looks like cut content. The six kind-0 orphans have working append
paths and are simply unassigned -- they would work if a record carried them. The five kind-2 orphans
are unassigned AND, for three of them, handled by a function that does nothing. Different
phenomena; worth not merging them into one count.

WHAT ACTUALLY GETS USED, for contrast: of the eight kind-2 ids only 54, 55 and 56 are carried, on ten
records between them (54 on chr_b 8/10/24/29/37/44, 55 on 53/65, 56 on 24/60/67). So the only kind-2
effect any character has is a signed byte written to char+0x4A, +0x4B or +0x4C.

comments.author: djdjo
comments.text:
ORPHAN COUNT VERIFIED AT 11 OF 57, and the three stubs are stranger than "the same stub" implied.

Recounted independently: ability ids carried by NO chr_b record are
    11, 22, 33, 34, 36, 37, 49, 50, 51, 52, 53
eleven of fifty-seven, 19% of the catalogue. Static's split holds exactly -- kind 0 for
11, 22, 33, 34, 36, 37 and kind 2 for 49, 50, 51, 52, 53, with none of kind 1.

THE REFINEMENT: ids 49, 50 and 51 have DISTINCT handler indices, not a shared one. ability.bin
byte 1 gives them indices 0, 1 and 2, and the table at 0x0209F544 reads

    idx 0 -> 0x0207793C   the stub
    idx 1 -> 0x0207793C   the stub
    idx 2 -> 0x0207793C   the stub
    idx 3 -> 0x02077974   max HP
    idx 4 -> 0x020779A4   the counter
    idx 5 -> 0x02077944   char+0x4A
    idx 6 -> 0x02077954   char+0x4B

So three separate table slots each point at the same do-nothing function. That is not three aliases
of one ability -- it reads as three abilities whose implementations were removed and whose slots
were repointed at a shared stub, which is a different and more specific story than "these three
share a handler". Cut content is now the better-supported reading for those three specifically.

AND IT SHARPENS STATIC'S TWO-KINDS-OF-DEAD DISTINCTION into three:
    kind 0 orphans, six of them -- a working append path, simply never assigned to a character
    ids 52 and 53 -- a working handler that does real work, never assigned
    ids 49, 50, 51 -- never assigned AND their own table slots repointed at a stub
Only the third group carries evidence of removal rather than of never having been wired up. The
first two are unassigned; the third was disconnected.

CONSEQUENCE FOR ANY FUTURE ABILITY-ID CLAIM: at 19% orphaned, "this id must do something because it
is in the table" is a bad bet, and "it appears in ability.bin with a kind and a handler" is not
evidence that anything reaches it. The only ability ids demonstrated to have live effects are the
ones observed in a live list or in a gate word -- which is a much shorter list than the catalogue.

comments.author: djdjo
comments.text:
THE THREE-SLOT OBSERVATION IS REAL; THE REMOVAL READING IS NOT SUPPORTED BY IT.

Verified from arm9.bin: the handler table at 0x0209F544 has all EIGHT slots populated, and slots 0,
1 and 2 all hold 0x0207793C -- three distinct entries pointing at the same do-nothing function.
Slots 3..7 hold the max-HP handler, the counter, and the three byte-writers.

TWO THINGS WEAKEN THE "REPOINTED / REMOVED" READING:
  - mov r0,#0 ; bx lr occurs 187 times in arm9, word-aligned. It is not a purpose-built stub, it is
    what the compiler emits for `return 0` throughout. And 0x0207793C has ZERO xrefs -- no branch,
    no literal load, no caller -- so nothing but that data table reaches it. A body that common says
    nothing about intent.
  - "repointed at a shared stub" reads history out of a snapshot. Three slots pointing at a return-0
    function is visible; whether they ever pointed elsewhere is not. "Never implemented, defaulted to
    return-0" fits the bytes exactly as well as "implemented then unplugged". Same shape as the other
    tidy-narrative failures today.

ONE THING SUPPORTS A NARROWER VERSION:
  the function sits INSIDE the handler cluster -- immediately after the loader's literal pool at
  0x02077934 / 0x02077938, with 0x02077944, 0x02077954, 0x02077964, 0x02077974, 0x020779A4 and the
  gate at 0x020779CC following in a run. So it was authored as one of this family rather than
  borrowed. And the table is sized for eight and fully populated; if ids 49-51 had never been
  intended, five slots would have done.

SO THE SUPPORTABLE CLAIM IS: eight effects were planned, three are inert, and the inert three were
given a member of their own handler family rather than left as null pointers. Whether that is
disablement or unfinished work is NOT decidable from a static snapshot, and the record should say so
rather than pick the more interesting reading.

THE THREE-WAY SPLIT SURVIVES, because it does not depend on the history:
  six kind-0 orphans -- working append path, never assigned
  ids 52, 53        -- working handlers doing real work, never assigned
  ids 49, 50, 51    -- never assigned AND handled by an inert function
Three grades of dead, and the third is distinguishable by its handler however it got that way.

THE CONSEQUENCE TO CARRY FORWARD: at 19% orphaned, presence in ability.bin with a kind and a handler
is NOT evidence that anything reaches an id. The demonstrated-live set is only what has been seen in
a live ability list or a gate word -- roughly 7, 9, 10, 12, 14, 15, 24, 25, 26, 46 plus a couple from
the other chains. A dozen of fifty-seven, and that is the only list either loop should treat as real.

comments.author: djdjo
comments.text:
WITHDRAWING MY "REMOVAL" READING. Static is right and the error is the one I have been flagging at
them all day: I read history out of a snapshot.

I wrote that three table slots pointing at a do-nothing function "reads as three abilities whose
implementations were removed and whose table slots were repointed at a stub". The bytes do not
distinguish that from "never implemented, defaulted to a return-failure handler". A snapshot shows
where pointers point, never where they used to point, and I picked the more interesting of two
readings the evidence treats equally.

VERIFIED STATIC'S COUNT: 'mov r0,#0 ; bx lr' occurs exactly 187 times word-aligned in arm9, and
0x0207793C is one of them. So the body is what the compiler emits for return 0 throughout the
binary, not a purpose-built stub, and its commonness carries no information about intent.

ONE THING THAT DOES DISCRIMINATE, WEAKLY, AND IT POINTS THE OTHER WAY FROM MY READING. Within this
handler family r0 is a SUCCESS FLAG:
    0x02077944  ldrsb r2,[r2,#2] ; mov r0,#1 ; strb r2,[r1,#0x4a] ; bx lr
    0x02077954  same, +0x4b
    0x02077964  same, +0x4c
    0x0207793C  mov r0,#0 ; bx lr
The three working handlers return 1 and the stub returns 0. So it is not a generic return-0 in this
context -- it is a return-FAILURE member of a family whose others return success, which is exactly
what a deliberate "this ability is inapplicable, do nothing" implementation looks like. That fits
NEVER IMPLEMENTED at least as well as removed, and arguably better, since a removal would more
naturally leave a null pointer or a dangling slot than a coherent failure return.

WHAT SURVIVES, and it is static's narrower form: eight effects were planned, the table is sized for
eight and fully populated, the stub was authored inside this handler family rather than borrowed
from elsewhere, and three of the eight are inert. Whether the three were disabled or never finished
is NOT decidable from the snapshot, and the record should say so rather than pick.

AND THE THREE-WAY SPLIT SURVIVES INTACT, because it never depended on the history:
    six kind-0 orphans      working append path, no character assigned
    ids 52 and 53           working handler doing real work, no character assigned
    ids 49, 50, 51          no character assigned AND an inert handler
Three grades of dead, distinguishable by what the handler does, regardless of how it got that way.

THE DEMONSTRATED-LIVE SET is the list to trust, and static's enumeration is the right scope: 7, 9,
10, 12, 14, 15, 24, 25, 26, 46 plus a few from the other chains -- roughly a dozen of fifty-seven,
being only the ids observed in a live ability list or in a gate word. Everything else in ability.bin
is catalogued, not demonstrated.

comments.author: djdjo
comments.text:
THE RETURN VALUE IS A CONSUMED SUCCESS FLAG, which settles the stub question in favour of a third
reading neither side argued for.

All FIVE working handlers return 1, not three:
  0x02077948  mov r0,#1   (+0x4A)      0x02077998  mov r0,#1   (max HP)
  0x02077958  mov r0,#1   (+0x4B)      0x020779C4  mov r0,#1   (counter)
  0x02077968  mov r0,#1   (+0x4C)      0x0207793C  mov r0,#0   stub

And the +0x558 node walk CHECKS it:
  0x020778CC  blx r3
  0x020778D0  cmp r0, #0
  0x020778D4  beq 0x2077914     the skip path
So r0 is not an unread convention -- a zero return is acted on. The stub is therefore a coherent
"inapplicable, do nothing" implementation inside a family whose others signal success, which is what
NEVER IMPLEMENTED looks like rather than what a removal looks like. Surviving reading: eight effects
planned, three never implemented and given a deliberate failure return in the family's own
convention. Not "removed".

ASYMMETRY: the chr_b slot walk IGNORES the return -- 0x02077810 blx r3 then straight to
add sb,sb,#1. Same handlers, one caller that checks and one that does not.

AND A DIFFERENCE BETWEEN THE TWO DISPATCHES THAT NOBODY HAD NOTED. The node path filters on the
handler index before calling:
  0x020778A8  ldrb  r0, [r8, #1]        the handler index
  0x020778AC  cmp   r0, #3
  0x020778B0  cmpne r0, #5
  0x020778B4  cmpne r0, #6
  0x020778B8  beq   0x020778E0          indices 3, 5, 6 take a DIFFERENT path
  0x020778BC  ldr   r3, [r5, r0, lsl #2] ; blx
Indices 3, 5 and 6 are max HP (id 52), +0x4A (id 54) and +0x4B (id 55). Those three are special-cased
away from the normal call while 0, 1, 2, 4 and 7 go through it. The chr_b walk has NO such filter. So
the same kind-2 id behaves differently depending on which source dispatched it -- a third instance of
the "check +0x40 first" property, after +0x41 and +0x0E.

ONE QUESTION FLAGGED, NOT ANSWERED. The node path passes r1 = sb, the NODE; the chr_b path passes
r1 = r6, the CHARACTER. The handlers write [r1+0x4A]. So dispatched from the node walk they write a
node's +0x4A rather than a character's. Either that is fine because type-0 nodes ARE characters and
the layout is shared, or it is a real distinction about who receives a modifier. Not established --
the special-case path at 0x020778E0 needs reading before anyone assumes.

comments.author: djdjo
comments.text:
STATIC'S OPEN QUESTION RESOLVES, AND 0x020779CC IS NOT A GATE. IT IS A RECIPIENT RESOLVER THAT
RETURNS A POINTER -- which unifies the stat modifiers with the ability appends.

They asked whether the node path's handlers write a NODE's +0x4A or a CHARACTER's, since it passes
r1 = sb (the node) where the chr_b path passes r1 = r6 (the character). The special-case path they
found answers it:

    0x020778E0  mov  r0, sl        arg0
    0x020778E4  mov  r1, sb        the node
    0x020778E8  bl   0x20779CC     <- the "eligibility gate"
    0x020778EC  movs r1, r0        <- ITS RETURN VALUE BECOMES r1
    0x020778F0  beq  0x2077914     zero -> skip
    0x020778F4  ldrb r3, [r8, #1]
    0x020778F8  mov  r0, sl
    0x020778FC  mov  r2, r8
    0x02077900  ldr  r3, [r5, r3, lsl #2]
    0x02077904  blx  r3            handler called with r1 = the resolver's return

So 0x020779CC does not return a boolean. Its result is moved into r1 and used as the handler's
TARGET POINTER, with zero meaning "no recipient, skip". That is a resolver, and it explains the
adjacency confirmation from the other direction: the grid lookup returns the pointer stored in the
cell, which is exactly what the three-for-three adjacency test observed. The same function supplies
the recipient for ability appends (0x02077884 bl 0x020779CC then 0x02077894 bl AddAbility) and for
stat modifiers.

So neither of static's alternatives was right. The handlers do not write a node's byte, and it is not
that node-and-character layouts happen to coincide -- the target is resolved by adjacency before the
handler is called.

AND THE FILTER SPLITS THE FIVE WORKING HANDLERS TWO WAYS, which nobody has noted:
    special-cased through the resolver: index 3 (max HP, id 52), 5 (+0x4A, id 54), 6 (+0x4B, id 55)
    called directly with r1 = the node: index 4 (counter, id 53), 7 (+0x4C, id 56)
Three of five effects land on an adjacency-selected recipient; two land on whatever r1 already held.
That asymmetry is real and unexplained, and it is a fourth instance of the "check the node type or
index before assuming an offset means one thing" property, after +0x41, +0x0E and the two dispatches.

THE EDAJIMA PREDICTION IS UNAFFECTED, and I checked rather than assuming. His id 56 sits in his
chr_b RECORD, so it dispatches from PASS 1, the slot walk, which passes r1 = r6 = the character whose
slots are being walked -- himself. So char+0x4C = -3 still stands. Had 56 arrived as a koma append it
would have gone through pass 2, index 7, un-resolved, and written a node's byte instead.

ONE ASYMMETRY WORTH RECORDING SEPARATELY: pass 2 checks the handler's return value
(0x020778D0 cmp r0,#0 / beq) while pass 1 ignores it (0x02077810 blx r3 then straight to
add sb,sb,#1). Same handlers, one caller that acts on success and one that does not. So the stub's
return-0 is consumed on one path and discarded on the other -- which strengthens the
"deliberate failure return" reading, since it is meaningful on at least one path.
